voyage.content: A weekly magazine that comprehensively covers the London gay scene with handy night by night listings available on-line and in print

voyage.name: Boyz Magazine
voyage.content: Which is published fortnightly and is freely available at most London gay venues, and contains listings of everything that is happening in all the major clubs in London and the South East.

voyage.name: London Gay and Lesbian Switchboard
voyage.content: This voluntary service has been operating since 1974 and as well as providing counselling they offer an incredibly thorough information service about Gay events, accommodation and businesses in London.

voyage.name: Bank of England
voyage.alt: The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street
voyage.content: See also: Bank of England Museum.

voyage.name: Mansion House
voyage.hours: Tue 2PM only, groups may book at other times
voyage.content: Official residence of the Lord Mayor of the City of London, completed in 1753.

voyage.name: Monument
voyage.price: Adults £4.50, children (5-15) £2.30, students and seniors (60+) £3.00; joint tickets for Tower Bridge and the Monument: adults £11.00, children £5.00, students and seniors £7.50
voyage.content: Designed by Sir Christopher Wren, this tall column (which can be ascended to get a great view) marks the alleged site where the Great Fire of London broke out in September 1666.

voyage.name: St Giles-without-Cripplegate
voyage.content: Medieval Grade I listed church. This church played a key role in the English Revolution and was the parish church of some of the most decisive Puritans: Oliver Cromwell was married and this is where John Milton was buried. It was the home of the Morning Exercises. The tower remains from the original building; the rest was destroyed in the Blitz but rebuilt based on the original plans.

voyage.name: St Sepulchre-without-Newgate
voyage.hours: Open Wed noon-3PM, services Sun 10:30AM, Tue 1PM & 6:30PM
voyage.content: Grade I listed Saxon church founded before the 12th century. The exterior was mostly constructed in the 15th century, and the interior in the 19th. The north side of the church houses a musician's chapel opened in 1955. In addition to the services, there are often evening (chargeable) concerts.

voyage.name: Old Bailey
voyage.content: This is probably the most famous criminal court in the world, and has been London's principal criminal court for centuries. It hears cases remitted to it from all over England and Wales as well as the Greater London area. The present building dates largely from 1907 (a new block was added from 1970 for more modern facilities) and stands on the site of the infamous medieval Newgate Gaol. The Central Criminal Court is

voyage.name: St Paul's Cathedral
voyage.content: The great domed cathedral of St Paul's, designed by Sir Christopher Wren to replace the Gothic medieval cathedral destroyed in 1666 in the Great Fire of London, was built between 1675–1710. Of the most famous London sights, St Paul's is the one most conveniently located for the Barbican. It's a significant building in British history, having been the site of the funerals of several British military leaders (Nelson, W

voyage.name: Tower Bridge
voyage.price: Bridge free; exhibition: adult £9.80, child (5–15) £4.20, senior/student £6.80; joint tickets for exhibition and the Monument: adults £11.00, children £5.00, students and seniors £7.50
voyage.content: Magnificent 19th-century bridge, decorated with high towers and featuring a drawbridge. The bridge opens several times each day to permit ships to pass through – timings are dependent on demand, and are not regularly scheduled. When Tower Bridge was built, the area to the west of it was a bustling port – necessitating a bridge that could permit tall boats to pass. Now the South Bank area sits to its west, and the reg

voyage.name: Tower of London
voyage.price: from £35.80, aged 5-17 £17.90, concession £28.50, entrance with gift aid is about 10% more.. If visiting multiple times or also visiting other Historic Royal Palaces it can be cheaper to buy an HRP annual membership
voyage.content: Founded by William the Conqueror in 1066, enlarged and modified by successive sovereigns, the Tower is today one of the world's most famous and spectacular fortresses and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Discover its 900-year history as a royal palace and fortress, prison and place of execution, mint, arsenal, menagerie and jewel house. In the winter you can skate on the dry moat. The Tower contains enough buildings and

voyage.name: All Hallows by the Tower
voyage.content: The oldest church in the City, founded by Saxon abbots in 675 AD.

voyage.name: St Bartholomew-the-Great
voyage.content: Founded in 1123, by jester-turned-monk Rahere, this Norman church is one of the oldest in London. It was damaged in the Dissolution but managed to escape both the Great Fire and the Blitz. This is a Grade I listed building. Tourists are welcome when services are not in progress and are charged an admission fee (which does not apply to those coming to pray or use the café).

voyage.name: St Botolph's Aldersgate
voyage.content: A medieval church that was rebuilt in the late 18th century, noted for its well-preserved interior. The former churchyard was converted into a public space in 1880, called Postman's Park as it was frequented by workers from the nearby Post Office headquarters.

voyage.name: Postman's Park
voyage.hours: 8AM–7PM or dusk (whichever is earlier). Closed Christmas Day, Boxing Day and New Year's Day
voyage.content: Postman's Park is three parks combined, bringing together the gardens of St Botolph's Aldersgate, Christ Church Greyfriars and St Leonard, Foster Lane. One of the largest parks in the City of London, Postman's Park contains the Memorial to Heroic Self Sacrifice; a memorial to ordinary people who died saving the lives of others and might otherwise have been forgotten.

voyage.name: St Lawrence Jewry
voyage.content: Properly St Lawrence Jewry next Guildhall, it is the official church of the Lord Mayor of London.

voyage.name: St Magnus the Martyr
voyage.content: Su Catholic Church of England with bells and smells (incense). There is an impressive model of the old London Bridge.

voyage.name: St Stephen Walbrook
voyage.content: Constructed 1672-9 to a design by Sir Christopher Wren and regarded as one of the finest Wren churches. The 63 feet (19 m) high dome is based on Wren's original design for St Paul's Cathedral. The circular altar is by the British sculptor Henry Moore, and the kneelers are designed by Patrick Heron. Free lunchtime concerts at 1PM on Tuesdays (except August). Free Organ recitals at 12:30PM on Fridays. Occasional art ex

voyage.name: Temple Church
voyage.hours: Varies, but approx.: Mon–Tue: 11AM–4PM; Wed: 2PM–4PM; Thu–Fri: 11AM–4PM
voyage.content: A small realm of serenity in the midst of the typical turmoil. It used to be the court of the Knights Templar. You can still visit the beautiful Romanesque church, which is one of the oldest ones in London (opened in 1185) and has connections to the order of Templars. The chancel of the church was built by Henry III. The church still serves the members of Gray's Inn and Lincoln's Inn and has frequent services open to

voyage.name: St Dunstan in the East
voyage.content: The ruins of a church dating back to Saxon times, rebuilt by St Dunstan in 950, destroyed in the Great Fire of London, and then rebuilt by Sir Christopher Wren in 1697. Most of the church was destroyed during the blitz, leaving only the tower (dating from Wren's time) and hollowed-out walls (from an 1817 reconstruction). The ruins are now overgrown with picturesque vines and trees, and were converted into a public ga

voyage.name: Museum of London
voyage.address: London Wall (NB: this is a street!)
voyage.content: Now permanently closed, will be replaced by new museum at the former Smithfield market site in 2026. The Museum of London Docklands remains open.

voyage.name: Guildhall Art Gallery and Roman Amphitheatre
voyage.content: The Guildhall Art Gallery houses the City Corporation's art collection, and also runs special exhibitions throughout the year. During construction of the modern gallery, workers discovered the ruins of London's Roman amphitheatre. The gallery was redesigned, and now the Amphitheatre is open to the public within the Guildhall Art Gallery itself and also free of charge.

voyage.name: Dr Johnson's House
voyage.price: adult £4.50, concession £3.50 (over 60, student or registered unemployed), child £1.50 (ages 5-17), family £10 (two adults and accompanying children), under 5s free. No debit or credit cards. National Trust Partner.
voyage.hours: October-April: Mon-Sat 11AM-5PM; May-September: Mon-Sat 11AM-5:30PM; closed Sundays, Bank Holidays
voyage.content: Dr Samuel Johnson was the highly distinguished 18th-century "man of letters", best known for his comprehensive English Dictionary of 1755, but also for his prolific output of poems, essays and novels. Something of a "hidden gem", this small, independent museum is dedicated to him—and, with its historic interiors, paintings and prints, personal effects and other exhibits—gives an impression of what it might have been

voyage.name: Bank of England Museum
voyage.content: Charts the history of the bank from 1694 to the present day. A highlight is the opportunity to handle a genuine bar of gold. Photography allowed, but no flash.

voyage.name: Barbican Centre
voyage.hours: Art Gallery: Mon-Fri 11AM–7PM 10AM–6PM, Sat–Sun 10AM–7PM; The Curve: Mon-Fri noon–7PM, Sat Sun 11AM–7PM
voyage.content: The largest arts centre in Europe, with music and theatre venues, and changing exhibitions.

voyage.name: London Mithraeum
voyage.hours: Tue-Sat 10AM-6PM, Sun and bank holidays noon-5PM
voyage.content: The London Mithraeum is a 3rd-century Roman mithraeum that was discovered in Walbrook during construction work in 1954. The entire site was relocated several times before being returned to its original site as part of the new Bloomberg building. This temple of the mystery god Mithras became perhaps the most famous 20th-century Roman discovery in London. In addition to the temple structure, there is a display of Roman

voyage.name: Barts Pathology Museum
voyage.content: Quirky medical museum. Only open to the public for scheduled evening events.

voyage.name: Barbican Conservatory
voyage.content: The second biggest greenhouse in London, containing over 2,000 species of tropical plants as well as birds and fish.

voyage.name: Blitz Plaque
voyage.content: The first of tens of thousands of bombs to hit London in World War II fell here in 1940.

voyage.name: Baltic Exchange
voyage.content: The world's main marketplace for ship broking.

voyage.name: London Wall
voyage.content: Remains of the wall that surrounded the City of London for almost two thousand years. The parts around the Barbican are mostly Tudor due to maintenance (Roman remains can be seen in and around the Tower of London). Other local remains are the and the .

voyage.name: Lloyds of London
voyage.content: The headquarters of world's most famous insurance market, housed in a revolutionary (at the time) bizarre, Matrix-like glass-and-steel building designed by Richard Rogers, with all support services (lifts, ventilation, etc.) suspended outside. Recognised as a masterpiece of exoskeleton architecture.

voyage.name: London Stock Exchange
voyage.content: After leaving its brutalist skyscraper on Old Broad St, the London Stock Exchange now resides on Paternoster Sq. Dating back to 1698, it is one of the world's oldest and largest stock markets.

voyage.name: London Bullion Market Association
voyage.content: This is where the world gold price is set twice a day.

voyage.name: London Metal Exchange
voyage.content: The LME is the leading centre for non-ferrous metals trading. It is also the last financial market in London which still retains open outcry trading.

voyage.name: London Stone
voyage.content: London Stone is a historic landmark housed in a public display case at 111 Cannon Street in the City of London. It is an irregular block of oolitic limestone measuring 53 × 43 × 30 cm (21″ × 17″ × 12″), the remnant of a once much larger object that had stood for many centuries on the south side of the street.

voyage.name: St Bride Printing Library
voyage.content: This specialist small library houses an impressive range of books on graphic design, typography, bookbinding and papermaking. The books cannot be borrowed but can be photocopied or photographed (with permission). An essential visit for any graphic design student.

voyage.name: The Gherkin
voyage.price: No entry, unless you have a restaurant reservation. Free to stand outside
voyage.content: Designed by one of Britain's leading architects, Sir Norman Foster, this curved glass skyscraper was the 2004 recipient of the Stirling Architectural Prize for Best Building. It was built on the site of the Baltic Exchange building, destroyed in 1992 by an IRA bomb which killed three. On the Bury Street side of the Gherkin by some black stone benches is the Tomb of the Unknown Girl for a teenaged Londoner who died 1,

voyage.name: Willis Building
voyage.content: Completed in 2008 opposite Lloyd's of London.

voyage.name: Leadenhall Building
voyage.content: Another Richard Rogers creation, nicknamed the Cheesegrater. Completed in 2014. Also opposite Lloyd's.

voyage.name: 20 Fenchurch Street
voyage.content: The unusual "walkie scorchie" profile of this skyscraper by Rafael Vinoly has seen it grab the headlines, as did the "death rays" caused by the sun's heat reflecting off the building onto the street below when it was first completed; car tyres melted and burst, and at least one man fried an egg using only the heat from the walkie talkie. Visitors can access the sky garden to see a magnificent view over the City and b

voyage.name: Fishmongers' Hall
voyage.content: The main headquarters of the Worshipful Company of Fishmongers and a Grade II* listed building.

voyage.name: Horizon 22
voyage.content: London's highest viewing platform that is free to the public. Sitting at the 58th floor of an office building, and the tallest building in City of London proper, it gives visitors a 300-degree view of London.

voyage.name: Barbican Architecture Tour
voyage.content: 90-minute tour of the beautifully ugly brutalist site.

voyage.name: Gresham College
voyage.content: Founded in 1597 as London's alternative higher education institution to Oxford and Cambridge, Gresham College continues to provide free public lectures every week during term time. Most lectures require no booking, with wonderful speakers delivering lectures on a wide range of interesting topics.

voyage.name: Lord Mayor's Show
voyage.content: The ceremony celebrates the appointment of the new Lord Mayor of the City of London. It is one of the great annual processions held in all London.

voyage.name: London Walks
voyage.content: Consider going along on one of the many excellent guided tours of the City, often with an evocative theme for example ghosts or Jack the Ripper.

voyage.name: London Night Tour
voyage.address: Departing from Coach stop 3, Bulleid Way

voyage.name: One New Change
voyage.content: The City's only modern shopping centre, which opened in October 2010. Includes around 60 shops and restaurants. It is situated right by St Paul's Cathedral and is in a small area of retailing, including Cheapside and the cobbled, old-fashioned Bow Lane. Both the freely accessible roof terrace, and the lifts to get there, offer excellent views of St Paul's.

voyage.name: Leadenhall Market
voyage.content: Worth visiting for its architecture and old-fashioned cobbled streets. It was used as a location in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone.

voyage.name: Royal Exchange
voyage.content: Situated opposite the Bank of England, the Exchange houses a number of upmarket outlets. Part of the exterior was featured in the film Bridget Jones' Diary (at the end, when Bridget runs after Mark along a snowy street).

voyage.name: Spitalfields Market
voyage.alt: Just outside the City and owned by the City of London Corporation
voyage.content: Once a large thriving market, it has slowly been shrunk to a third of its size by development in the area. It features a good variety of clothing, crafts and food stalls/shops. Rather promisingly sellers have set up another market in a new space off Hanbury St nearby. Visit 66/68 Bell Lane nearby to see a wealthy merchant's house, rumour has it John Lennon once played on the roof of this building with Yoko Ono.

voyage.name: Tesco Express
voyage.content: Small, local branch of the supermarket

voyage.name: Tesco Express
voyage.content: Small, local branch of the supermarket

voyage.name: Sainsbury's Local
voyage.content: Small, local branch of the supermarket. In a pedestrian square near St. Paul's Cathedral.

voyage.name: Assenheims 56
voyage.content: South American cuisine

voyage.name: Pilpel
voyage.content: A falafel restaurant.

voyage.name: Eataly London
voyage.content: An Italian food hall and eatery opened in 2021 along the lines of the Turin original. It's east side of Liverpool St station.

voyage.name: Polo Bar
voyage.content: An unpretentious cafe serving fried breakfasts and similar basic food 24 hr a day, and a great place for a late snack after you leave the Eat & Drink. Liverpool St is a safe area anyway but you cannot get safer than this for a late night meal, as at night you'll often see police from the nearby City of London police station. There are no toilets, however, so you need to use those at nearby Liverpool St Station.

voyage.name: Smiths of Smithfields
voyage.content: Smiths of Smithfield is a Grade II listed four-floor restaurant serving great British food.

voyage.name: Wood Street Bar and Restaurant
voyage.content: Real ale, nice food and a relaxed atmosphere.

voyage.name: Apulia
voyage.content: Italian restaurant.

voyage.name: Duck and Waffle
voyage.content: All day dining on the 40th floor of the Heron Tower. Popular in the very late night for a bite after going out and waiting to watch the sunrise over the rest of London.

voyage.name: Angler
voyage.price: Tasting menu £100 / £170 with wine pairing. À la carte mains £24-£30 (April 2021)
voyage.hours: Wed 6PM-9:30PM; Thu Fri noon-2:30PM, 6PM-9:30PM; Sat noon-3PM, 6PM-9:30PM; Sun noon-3PM
voyage.content: One Michelin-starred British seafood restaurant with views over the City.

voyage.name: Hand & Shears
voyage.content: Grade II listed historic pub

voyage.name: The Hope
voyage.content: Grade II listed pub

voyage.name: The Jugged Hare
voyage.content: A gastropub modelled on a traditional countryside drinking establishment, with a hunting theme. The tables are actually old whisky barrels and the décor features several stuffed animals and trophies. Completing the pattern, the food is heavily game-based, with some seafood. Their titular signature dish is an 18th-century stew recipe.

voyage.name: Old Red Cow
voyage.hours: Mon–Thu noon–11PM; Fri–Sat noon-midnight; Sun noon–10:30PM
voyage.content: Small pub that serves real ale and craft beer from both major and local breweries.

voyage.name: Dirty Dick's
voyage.content: One of the better known pubs (although definitely no tourist trap) near Liverpool St, supposedly named after a Georgian dandy who let himself go on the death of his fiancée.

voyage.name: The Old Doctor Butler's Head
voyage.content: This claims to be one of London's oldest pubs, tracing it history to 1610, although it has been rebuilt since then. The eponymous Doctor Butler was a purveyor of "medicinal ale" who was appointed court physician to James I. Pubs selling his beer were allowed to display his portrait, hence the name of the establishment.

voyage.name: The Crosse Keys
voyage.content: Part of the JD Wetherspoons chain in a converted bank. As is usual for the chain, it is fairly cheap with decent food and drink. The ex-bank building makes this pub a little grander and more spacious than most.

voyage.name: The Hung Drawn & Quartered
voyage.content: Fullers Pub

voyage.name: Lamb Tavern
voyage.content: One of several pubs in Leadenhall Market where you can listen to insurance brokers from nearby Lloyd's talk business.

voyage.name: The Ship
voyage.content: A Nicolson's pub rebuilt after it was burnt down during the fire of London.

voyage.name: The Sterling
voyage.content: A central bar that resides in the heart of the Gherkin. Catch your breath from the bustle of the City and enjoy a bit of al fresco dining. Food and drink available.

voyage.name: The Blackfriar
voyage.content: A pub with an art deco church built inside.

voyage.name: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese
voyage.content: An old City pub establishment, rebuilt shortly after the Great Fire of 1666. All the monarchs who have reigned in England during the pub's time are written by the main door.

voyage.name: The Sugar Loaf
voyage.content: Pub that is popular with City workers. You will often find a crowd spilling out into the adjacent pedestrian area, particularly on Tuesdays-Thursdays when workers tend to come into the office more.

voyage.name: Savage Garden
voyage.content: Cocktail bar with 360 views of London

voyage.name: Vinoteca
voyage.content: Wine bar and shop.

voyage.name: Fabric
voyage.content: A massive club (think cathedral scale) that provides a more underground version of Ministry of Sound and hosts some of the biggest names in dance music, from Goldie to David Holmes to the Scratch Perverts. There are always big queues, so get down early if you can.

voyage.name: The Hoxton, Shoreditch
voyage.content: 210 room hotel, with some cheaper "shoebox" rooms.

voyage.name: YHA London St Paul's
voyage.price: Dorm from £18.95 including breakfast. 6 rooms for 2 people and 3 singles
voyage.content: Small hostel converted from one of the City's oldest buildings. Cheap for Central London accommodation, range of room sizes, basic facilities.

voyage.name: Apex City of London Hotel
voyage.content: Located in the City close to the Tower of London. 179 luxury bedrooms and suites, restaurant, bar and gym. Free fast speed Wi-fi.

voyage.name: Apex Temple Court Hotel
voyage.content: 184 spacious luxury bedrooms and suites, bar, restaurant, executive lounge and gym. Free fast speed Wi-fi.

voyage.name: Queen Street St Paul's Apartments
voyage.content: These serviced apartments are situated in the centre of the City area of London, with Walbrook, Bank and Monument being a short walk away. The neighbouring streets are filled with cafes, restaurants and local shops, ensuring your stay is both enjoyable and convenient.

voyage.name: Apex London Wall Hotel
voyage.content: Close to the Bank of England and Liverpool Street Station. 89 luxury bedrooms and suites, bar, restaurant and gym. Free fast speed Wi-fi.

voyage.name: Andaz London Liverpool Street
voyage.content: A concept casual luxury hotel. No two bedrooms the same.

voyage.name: SACO Apartments – Aldgate
voyage.content: A grade II listed Victorian building. A great alternative to hotels for those travelling on business.

voyage.name: CitizenM Tower of London
voyage.content: Slick modern hotel, try for a room with a view of Tower of London. No dogs.

voyage.name: Citadines Holborn-Covent Garden London
voyage.content: Located a short walk from Covent Garden. Each air-conditioned apartment houses a bathroom with a separate toilet, a separate kitchen area and Internet access.

voyage.name: Malmaison London
voyage.content: Great location with attentive staff.

voyage.name: South Place Hotel
voyage.content: Chic city hotel with good grub in the Chop House and great dining in the Angler's Restaurant.

voyage.name: Palace of Westminster
voyage.alt: more widely known as the Houses of Parliament
voyage.content: On the UNESCO World Heritage List, the Palace of Westminster is the seat of Parliament in the United Kingdom. It's often termed the "Mother of All Parliaments" - an exaggeration, but perhaps only a slight one. The present building largely dates from the 19th century when it was rebuilt following a fire in a splendid example of Victorian neo-Gothic architecture. The House of Commons (elected Members of Parliament or M

voyage.name: St. Stephen's Hall
voyage.content: Upon entry, you pass through a metal detector, and are very thoroughly searched. You then proceed into St. Stephen's Hall, where you are seated to wait for admission. A representative of the Sergeant-at-Arms gives you a slip of paper to write your name and address on.

voyage.name: House of Commons Strangers' Gallery
voyage.content: When called, you proceed from St. Stephen's Hall to the Central Hall, and then upstairs. You must leave all items (bags, cameras, mobile phones, writing and written material) outside and then proceed through to the Strangers' Gallery. Upon entry, you can pick up a copy of the proceedings being discussed in the House that day. You should be quiet, anything above a whisper may lead to you being asked to leave. After le

voyage.name: House of Lords Strangers' Gallery
voyage.content: If you head away from the Commons, you pass along a corridor towards the Lords. If you ask to visit the Strangers' Gallery, a representative of Black Rod asks you to complete another slip of paper with your name and address. You then proceed up a staircase to the Lords Strangers' Gallery. Again, all items need to be left outside. Of the two chambers, the Lords is by far the more impressive, featuring the stunning thr

voyage.name: Westminster Hall
voyage.content: After visiting the two Houses, visitors pass back through St. Stephen's Hall, and through Westminster Hall. Westminster Hall is one of the few areas of Parliament in which photography is permitted, and it is a very impressive place, dating back to the 9th century. Plaques on the floor mark where the bodies of deceased members of the royal family and other distinguished individuals granted the privilege by the British

voyage.name: State Opening of Parliament
voyage.content: Probably the most colourful event in the UK's legislative calendar, this takes place in May or June every year, or after a general election, when the King travels to the Houses of Parliament to open the new parliamentary session. During this event, the Lords, Speaker of the House of Commons, and other office holders can be seen dressed in their ceremonial robes, and there is always an elaborate procession when the Ki

voyage.name: Summer Opening
voyage.content: While the Houses are in recess, the Palace of Westminster is generally closed - apart from the long Summer recess, during which tours are run through the building, led by Parliamentary employees. Popularity of these tours means you're best advised to book in advance - a stall erected on the green opposite the Palace of Westminster on Millbank sells tickets in the Summer.

voyage.name: Elizabeth Tower
voyage.alt: commonly referred to as Big Ben
voyage.content: Strictly limited numbers of tickets are available to climb the Elizabeth Tower, which was renamed from Clock Tower in 2012. It contains the Great Bell, commonly known as Big Ben. British visitors should write to their Member of Parliament to request tickets. Unfortunately there are no tours for overseas visitors.

voyage.name: The Jewel Tower
voyage.hours: daily in summer, Sat, Sun only in winter.
voyage.content: This small tower across the road from the Houses of Parliament is the only part of the original Palace of Westminster still standing. While it is overshadowed in splendour by the surrounding buildings, it's well worth a visit, and has good displays about the early history of Westminster.

voyage.name: Buckingham Palace
voyage.hours: Summer opening: 31 Jul-29 Sep 9:45AM-3:45PM (closed rest of year)
voyage.content: The main residence of His Majesty King Charles III, Her Royal Highness Queen Camilla, and latterly of HM Queen Elizabeth II. In the summer, 19 State Rooms are open to the public. Places are strictly limited, and it might not be possible to just turn up and get a ticket for a specific entry time, visitors should book in advance to ensure admission.

voyage.name: St James's Palace
voyage.hours: Not open to the public, but can be seen from the street
voyage.content: The most senior of the Royal palaces in London (built between 1531 and 1536) and the official seat of the monarch.

voyage.name: St James's Church, Piccadilly
voyage.content: Church in Piccadilly designed by Sir Christopher Wren in 1684. It has a magnificent organ case and baptismal font by Grinling Gibbons.

voyage.name: Henry VII Lady Chapel
voyage.content: Described as "the wonder of the entire world", this chapel at the eastern end of Westminster Abbey is a breathtakingly beautiful masterpiece of medieval architecture.

voyage.name: St. Margaret's Church
voyage.content: St. Margaret's is the church of the British Parliament, more specifically, the parish church of the House of Commons.

voyage.name: Westminster Abbey
voyage.price: Adult £31 (with one child free), senior or student with full-time student card 65+ £28, children 6-17 £14, children under 6 free
voyage.hours: Abbey admission: Mon-Fri 9:30AM-3:30PM, Sat 9:30AM-3PM, Sun open for worship only, the Abbey closes 1 hr after last admission; The Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries: Mon-Fri 10AM-3PM, Sat 9:30AM-3PM
voyage.content: The Abbey is the traditional scene for the coronation of British monarchs and the burial place of many past kings and queens. The Abbey contains a good gift shop and the Cellarium Café, which traces its history to the 14th century, is a good place to buy a noontime meal. Westminster Abbey is usually open to visitors from Monday to Saturday throughout the year. On Sundays and religious holidays such as Easter and Chri

voyage.name: Tate Britain
voyage.price: Free (though there is a charge for temporary exhibitions)
voyage.content: This gallery houses the Tate collection of British art from 1500 through to contemporary art. A side wing collects together the gallery's collection of paintings by Turner, including some stunning seascapes. Temporary exhibitions are exceedingly varied: examples include exhibitions of Turner's paintings of Venice and the work of photographer Wolfgang Tillmans. The best known exhibition is the Turner Prize, consists o

voyage.name: Green Park
voyage.content: In contrast to the other Royal Parks in the area, Green Park can seem a little plain. It has no lakes or buildings and few monuments. It is still a pleasant green, lightly wooded, area in the centre of London, neighbouring two other parks and Buckingham Palace.

voyage.name: St. James's Park
voyage.content: The oldest of the Royal Parks of London.

voyage.name: Wellington Arch
voyage.hours: Interior access daily: Apr–Sep 10AM–6PM; Oct 10AM–5PM; Nov–Mar 10AM–4PM
voyage.address: Apsley Way, Hyde Park Corner, W1J 7JZ
voyage.content: The Arch was designed in the 1820s by Decimus Burton as a Roman-style triumphal arch to commemorate victory in the Napoleonic Wars; although money ran out before it was completed. Adrian Jones' chariot statue on the top, "Peace descending on the Quadriga of War", was added in 1912. The original equestrian statue, added in 1846, was widely disliked and now stands in Aldershot. The arch is now owned by English Heritage

voyage.name: Duke of Wellington
voyage.content: Equestrian statue of the Iron Duke, with four soldiers at each corner of the pedestal, representing regiments that fought under him: a Grenadier, Scottish Highlander, Irish Dragoon, and Welsh Fusilier. The bronze came from melting down captured French cannons.

voyage.name: Royal Artillery Memorial
voyage.content: A stone howitzer by World War I veteran Charles Sargeant Jagger

voyage.name: Australian War Memorial
voyage.content: Created by Tonkin Zulaikha Greer and Janet Laurence to remember the Australians who died in both world wars. Made from Australian granite.

voyage.name: Machine Gun Corps Memorial
voyage.content: A statue of David holding Goliath's sword by Francis Derwent Wood commemorating the dead of the World War I corps.

voyage.name: New Zealand Memorial
voyage.content: Sixteen cruciform bronze pillars designed by Paul Dibble and John Hardwick-Smith.

voyage.name: RAF Bomber Command Memorial
voyage.content: Built of Portland stone and dedicated to the aircrews of Allied nations under Bomber Command during World War II.

voyage.name: Thomas Cubitt
voyage.address: Corner of Denbigh St and St George's Drive

voyage.name: Westminster Cathedral
voyage.price: Cathedral: free. Tower: £6 adults, £3 concessions, Treasures Exhibition £2
voyage.content: Worth a quick visit if you are passing. The brick and stone neo-Byzantine Catholic Cathedral (not to be confused with the much more famous Westminster Abbey) is near Victoria Station, just off Victoria Street. Construction started in 1895, and some of the interior is still unfinished. The Treasures of Westminster Cathedral exhibition is inexpensive and worthwhile for learning the history of the cathedral, there are i

voyage.name: Banqueting House
voyage.price: £4, students (with ID) and seniors (60+) £3.00, children 5-16 £2.60, under 5 free
voyage.hours: Mon-Sat 10AM-5PM, closed Sun, Bank Holidays and 24 Dec-1 Jan (inclusive); The Banqueting House is liable to close at short notice for government functions, telephone to check before you travel
voyage.content: Designed and built in 1619-1622 by the Neo-Classical architect Inigo Jones, The Banqueting House is now all that remains of Whitehall Palace, the sovereign's principal residence from 1530-1698 when most of it was destroyed by fire. Renowned for its architecture and paintings (by Rubens, among others), the building is also famous for being the scene of Charles I's execution in 1649 at the end of the English Civil War.

voyage.name: Cabinet War Rooms and Churchill Museum
voyage.price: Adult from £25; children 5-15 from £12.50, under 5 free; seniors and students £15.20; group concessions available
voyage.address: Clive Steps, King Charles St, SW1A 2AQ
voyage.content: A branch of the Imperial War Museum, the Cabinet War Rooms preserves the underground corridors and rooms from which Churchill and the cabinet directed the war against Hitler and the Nazis, maintained almost exactly as they were left in 1945. In 1984, IWM opened the rooms to the public for the first time. In 2005, the attached Churchill Museum was opened as the world's first permanent museum dedicated to the life and

voyage.name: Downing Street
voyage.content: Site of the London residences for the Prime Minister (No. 10) and the Chancellor (No. 11).

voyage.name: Whitehall
voyage.content: This street runs between Parliament Square and Trafalgar Square, and is the site of several British government buildings. Horseguards Parade, and the heavily guarded entrance to Downing Street (see above) are on the west side. Banqueting House is on the east side. In the centre of the street sits the Cenotaph, a war memorial erected following World War I, which is the centre of the annual Remembrance Day ceremony on

voyage.name: Changing of the Guard
voyage.hours: May-Jul 11:30AM daily; for other times, see website
voyage.content: Each morning between May and July at 11:30AM the guard changes outside Buckingham Palace. The rest of the year, the guard changes on alternate days, weather permitting. A board is placed outside the palace in the morning to say whether the Changing of the Guard ceremony will take place or not. There is no charge to view the Changing of the Guard—simply turn up and stand at the fence in front of the Palace, but it is

voyage.name: Changing of the Guard
voyage.content: Each morning the guard is also changed at Horse Guards Parade. As this changing of the guard is less famous than the Buckingham Palace affair, the crowds are usually smaller; plus there are no railings here to spoil the view. The ceremony does not take place in very wet weather. The cavalry are based at Hyde Park Barracks and can be seen proceeding through the park, under the Wellington Arch, along Constitution Hill

voyage.name: Dismounting Ceremony
voyage.content: In the late afternoon at Horse Guards an officer will inspect the guards, after which the mounted sentries return their horses to the stables for the night. They are replaced by two dismounted sentries. This ceremony was born as a punishment detail in 1894 but it was retained as a tradition when the 100-year punishment period ended in the 1990s.

voyage.name: Trooping the Colour
voyage.price: About £20 if successful in the ballot
voyage.hours: Held annually on a Sat in June, beginning around 10AM
voyage.content: A ceremony performed by regiments of the British and Commonwealth armies to mark the official birthday of the King. The King and his family travel by carriage down The Mall from Buckingham Palace to Horse Guards Parade, where they inspect the troops and then the entire Household Division performs a march past the King as he receives their salute. Tickets to Horse Guards Parade are awarded by ballot but the parade alo

voyage.name: Major General's Review
voyage.price: Free but tickets are still required.
voyage.hours: The Sat two weeks before Trooping the Colour; usually in late May
voyage.content: Tickets are made available by the same ballot as Trooping the Colour.

voyage.name: Colonel's Review
voyage.hours: The Sat the week before Trooping the Colour
voyage.content: Tickets are made available by the same ballot as Trooping the Colour.

voyage.name: Beating Retreat
voyage.hours: Held on the Wed and Thu evenings before Trooping the Colour
voyage.content: This began as a 16th-century tradition for recalling troops to a castle at sunset before the gates closed. Today, the ceremony has evolved into a military pageant of music and precision drilling, while also serving as practice for military bands. The proceeds from ticket sales go to charity.

voyage.name: Cineworld Haymarket
voyage.content: Slightly off the main area for cinemas and entertainment around Leicester Square and Theatreland this cinema offers projections of recent movies on three large screens.

voyage.name: Vue Piccadilly
voyage.content: Multi screen of the Vue network very close to Piccadilly Circus.

voyage.name: St John's Smith Square
voyage.address: St John's Smith Square, London, SW1P 3HA
voyage.content: Former baroque church by Thomas Archer. From the 1960s, converted into a concert hall and featuring world class classical music performers with daily concerts from September to July.

voyage.name: Free Walking Tours
voyage.content: There are a number of regular free walking tours in London but the most well known leaves from The Duke of Wellingon Arch twice daily and covers many of the important sights in Westminster. Duration about 2½ hours.

voyage.name: Cardinal Place
voyage.content: High street shops like Marks & Spencer and a selection of chain restaurants.

voyage.name: Les Senteurs
voyage.content: Specialist perfumery.

voyage.name: Retromania
voyage.content: Charity shop specialising in vintage and retro clothing.

voyage.name: Hilditch & Key
voyage.content: With another branch at

voyage.name: Budd Shirts
voyage.content: Budd, established in 1910, is the only Jermyn Street shirtmaker to still have a bespoke cutting room on site, where shirts are still made.

voyage.name: Franco Manca
voyage.content: Pizza

voyage.name: Westminster Cathedral Cafe
voyage.content: The cafe in the basement of Westminster Cathedral is one of the cheapest places to have lunch in the area. Simple tasty hot lunches (Jacket Potatoes etc) cost under £5. Get in through the Cathedral main entrance.

voyage.name: The Laughing Halibut
voyage.content: The classic shop for fish and chips.

voyage.name: Pataka
voyage.address: Grosvenor Gardens House, 50-52 Buckingham Palace Rd, SW1W 0RN
voyage.content: Opened in 2021, Pataka serves modern Indian food.

voyage.name: Cardinal Place
voyage.content: A selection of chain restaurants together in the shopping centre. Includes Browns Bar & Brasserie, La Tasca, Leon, Nandos, Royal Quarter Café, Wagamama, and Zizzi.

voyage.name: The Ebury Restaurant and Wine Bar
voyage.content: French/European restaurant.

voyage.name: Seafresh
voyage.content: Fish and chips restaurant and takeaway.

voyage.name: Oliviomare
voyage.hours: Mon–Fri noon–2:30PM, 7–11PM; Sat noon–3PM, 7–11PM; Sun noon-3PM, 7–10:30PM
voyage.content: Sardinian seafood restaurant. Part of a small, local chain found only in this area.

voyage.name: The Orange
voyage.content: Modern gastropub, you can eat in the ground-floor bar but the best dining is in the first-floor restaurant. With four comfy en suite bedrooms.

voyage.name: Quaglinos
voyage.content: Owned by famed designer Terence Conrad, it serves standard food with a menu that changes frequently. It features live jazz every night and on Sunday lunch.

voyage.name: Zizzi
voyage.content: A cozy Italian restaurant next to the Westminster Cathedral and Victoria Station, with a huge wood fired pizza oven that creates a welcome atmosphere on its own. Pizzas between £12 - £16, and various pasta dishes and salads. Fairly large portions, so one main dish per person suffices for a meal. Suitable for families with kids.

voyage.name: The Cinnamon Club
voyage.address: The Old Westminster Library, 30–32 Great Smith St, SW1P 3BU
voyage.content: Indian restaurant. Housed in a converted Grade II listed library.

voyage.name: Hunan
voyage.content: Chinese restaurant with no menu. Diners tell the staff what they don't like and how spicy they want it; the kitchen prepares a range of dishes to match. The food comes in a long series of tiny portions.

voyage.name: Wiltons
voyage.content: Oyster bar, game and seafood restaurant. Traditional fine English dining in a restaurant established in 1742.

voyage.name: The Antelope
voyage.hours: Mon–Thu & Sat noon–11PM; Fri noon–12:30PM, Sun noon–10PM
voyage.content: Traditional pub with many original features preserved from its Georgian origin.

voyage.name: The Grenadier
voyage.content: An oddly quiet and secluded pub in the centre of the city due to being tucked away in a side street of another side street. It was built in 1720 as an officer's mess for the 1st Regiment of Foot Guards and became a pub in 1818. The pub is said to be haunted by the ghost of a junior officer who was caught cheating at cards and flogged to death.

voyage.name: The Star Tavern
voyage.content: One of only two London pubs (and seven nationally) to feature in every edition of CAMRA's Good Beer Guide since its first publication; see The Buckingham Arms for the other one. The pub has a seedy past—it was infamous as a hangout for gang bosses and crime lords in the 1950s and 60s, and the Great Train Robbery was planned here, and celebrities of the era would come to socialise with the criminals. Today it is a saf

voyage.name: Duke of Wellington
voyage.content: Oak-panelled corner pub.

voyage.name: Golden Lion
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri noon-11PM Sat noon-6PM Sun noon-9PM

voyage.name: Old Red Lion
voyage.content: A small freehouse, hidden down a passageway, with leaded windows and a red lion statue

voyage.name: The Red Lion, Mayfair
voyage.content: A beautiful Fullers pub with loads of mirrors.

voyage.name: Fortnum & Mason
voyage.content: An upmarket grocery store, with royal connections. Buy tea and drink tea here.

voyage.name: The Rose Lounge
voyage.content: French style afternoon tea.

voyage.name: CASK Pub & Kitchen
voyage.content: One of RateBeer's Top 50 bars in the world, and only one of two in the UK (see The Craft Beer Company in Clerkenwell for the other). A specialist beer bar with a regularly changing selection of real ales and craft beer casks, plus a larger assortment of local and international bottles. Monday to Saturday, gourmet burgers are served by Forty Burgers; with traditional British roasts on Sundays.

voyage.name: Morpeth Arms
voyage.content: Victorian pub built on the site of the cells of Millbank Prison, briefly Britain's National Penitentiary before being downgraded to a holding facility for convicts sentenced to transportation to Australia. The pub is said to be haunted by the ghosts of prisoners who didn't last long enough for the journey. For the living, the pub is next to the bank of the Thames and very close to the Tate gallery.

voyage.name: The Albert
voyage.content: A nice, but often crowded, traditional pub, dating back to the 1860s, named in honour of Queen Victoria's husband. Portraits of British prime ministers, many of them signed, hang on the stairwell, and Chelsea pensioners (British war veterans) can often be seen propping up the bar.

voyage.name: The Cask and Glass
voyage.content: Small traditional pub (one of the smallest in central London, in fact). Good beers and quaint interior.

voyage.name: Fox & Hounds
voyage.content: Youngs Pub

voyage.name: Wetherspoons
voyage.content: A pub that doesn't even have its own name and may be missed by many of the 200,000 commuters and travellers who pass it each day, this place nevertheless serves good beer and food (it's part of the J D Wetherspoon chain). There is additional seating on the balconies on either side of the pub. Given its location, it also displays departure boards on its own screens.

voyage.name: Windsor Castle
voyage.content: Sam Smiths pub with plenty of etched glass.

voyage.name: The Willow Walk
voyage.content: Part of the J D Wetherspoon chain of pubs, just outside the East side of Victoria Station, a few doors down from the Apollo Victoria Theatre. Serves Real Ale and good food. Entrances on both Wilton Rd and Vauxhall Bridge Rd.

voyage.name: The Admiralty
voyage.content: A Fullers Pub that has been decked out like an 18th century British warship.

voyage.name: The Buckingham Arms
voyage.content: One of only two London pubs (and seven nationally) to feature in every edition of CAMRA's Good Beer Guide since its first publication; see The Star Tavern for the other one. The building is a refitted early Victorian pub.

voyage.name: Horse & Guardsman
voyage.content: A McMullen pub at the top of Whitehall, close to Trafalgar Sq. with a cavalry theme worth going in for the wall sized picture of the Scots Greys. Serves a good range of cask beers.

voyage.name: The Red Lion
voyage.content: A good place to see politicians and political commentators. The pub television shows (muted) debates from the House of Commons, and division bell rings here to summon Members of Parliament to vote on important issues in Parliament.

voyage.name: The Speaker
voyage.content: A pub for local workers, including many civil servants and the odd Parliamentarian. The Parliament theme includes political caricatures on the walls. Markets itself as a real pub, with no fruit machines, music or television screens. Guest beers change every month.

voyage.name: St Stephen's Tavern Pub
voyage.content: Victorian pub established in 1875 directly opposite the Palace of Westminster and the closest pub to "Big Ben" (from which it gets its name—while now officially known as Elizabeth Tower, Victorian journalists nicknamed it St Stephen's Tower). Often busy with tourists and other visitors to Parliament.

voyage.name: The Wellington
voyage.content: Located in quiet area. Internet access available. 10 min from Victoria Station.

voyage.name: DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel London—Westminster
voyage.content: A boutique hotel. Offers a restaurant, bar, meeting venue and event offers.

voyage.name: Corinthia Hotel London
voyage.content: Comfortable hotel with rooms, suites and penthouses.

voyage.name: Eccleston Square Hotel
voyage.content: Smart hotel, lots of gadgets, but some rooms very small.

voyage.name: St Ermin's Hotel
voyage.content: Small but well appointed rooms in a convenient location near Westminster Abbey.

voyage.name: Luna & Simone Hotel
voyage.content: Small yet comfortable hotel with friendly staff.

voyage.name: Sanctuary House Hotel
voyage.content: Small hotel in a lovely old building close to Westminster Abbey, part of a popular Fullers pub.

voyage.name: Lime Tree Hotel
voyage.content: Remarkable to find a comfy modern mid-range B&B in pricey Belgravia. Lots of stairs! No children under 5 or dogs.

voyage.name: The Ritz Hotel
voyage.content: One of London's great hotels for more than a century, overlooking Green Park. If you cannot afford to stay here (likely), then a splurge on afternoon tea in the opulent Louis XIV Palm Court is recommended (£54-£90). Dress appropriately - a jacket and tie for gentlemen; smart attire and proper shoes for everyone - otherwise you will not get past the door.

voyage.name: Artist Residence London
voyage.content: Offbeat stylish hotel with ten rooms and two suites, good restaurant.

voyage.name: St James Court Hotel
voyage.content: Four star hotel close to Buckingham Palace and The Houses of Parliament. Has three restaurants, Spa, and Gym.

voyage.name: The Grosvenor
voyage.content: Next door to Victoria railway and tube station.

voyage.name: St James’s Hotel & Club
voyage.content: A luxury townhouse hotel in a former diplomats' club, swell comfort, service and dining. No dogs.

voyage.name: The Goring
voyage.content: Very upscale Edwardian hotel in Belgravia, great cuisine. Assistance dogs only.

voyage.name: The Stafford
voyage.content: Opulent hotel in a historic townhouse overlooking Green Park, great dining. No dogs.

voyage.name: Hotel 41
voyage.content: Top calibre hotel for comfort, service and cuisine, redolent of old money, and overlooking those po' folks at Buckingham Palace who wish they could afford to stay here.

voyage.name: British Library
voyage.content: The official book depository of the United Kingdom, holding a copy of every book ever printed here, and a wide variety of periodicals. No less than 150 million items catalogued and there is an unimaginable 625 km of shelving! Visitors may not use the library unless they have proof of identity, home address, and a genuine need to use a specific item, but there is a free "Treasures of the British Library" exhibition ch

voyage.name: Camley Street Natural Park
voyage.content: A 2-acre nature reserve amid the industrial wasteland just north of King's Cross Station. This lovely little park gives visitors interested in nature the opportunity to learn about the work of the London Wildlife Trust who administer this and 26 other reserves in London. This is the only one in the centre of the city.

voyage.name: Jewish Museum
voyage.price: Adult £7.50, senior (60+) or student or unemployed or disabled £5.50, child (5-16) £3.50, free with National Art Pass or London Pass of child under 5
voyage.content: In 2010, it reopened after a renovation with a modern extension. Exhibitions on the long history of the Jewish community in London. Well laid out and interesting.

voyage.name: Regent's Canal
voyage.content: You can walk or cycle along the canal through east London all the way to the Thames (3 hr). The St. Pancras lock is directly north of St Pancras station. Regent's Canal was once a lifeline for trade and industry in London with narrowboats and barges ferrying goods to and from North London. The canal winds its way from the Grand Union Canal near Paddington in West London, past Regent's Park, Camden, Islington and Mile

voyage.name: St. Pancras Old Church and cemetery
voyage.content: Hidden away behind St. Pancras railway station is what is believed to be one of the oldest sites of Christian worship in England. There has been a church on the site since at least around the year 314. The current church is mostly a 19th-century structure, but it contains some traces of an older Norman structure. Surrounding the church is a cemetery, today transformed into a public park that contains a memorial to ph

voyage.name: St. Pancras International railway station
voyage.content: Ornate Neo-Gothic architecture, used in the Harry Potter films.

voyage.name: Cecil Sharp House
voyage.address: 2 Regent's Park Rd, Primrose Hill, London NW1 7AY
voyage.content: English Folk Dancing.

voyage.name: Shaw Theatre
voyage.content: Theatre named after George Bernard Shaw and famous for showing high-quality non-mainstream productions.

voyage.name: The Lock Market
voyage.content: Many stores mainly focused around music and clothing. This is the market most people mean when they talk about the "Camden Market".

voyage.name: The Stables Market
voyage.hours: Some shops open all week, but most stalls only Sat Sun 9AM-6PM
voyage.content: This is the largest of Camden's market areas, featuring hundreds of stalls selling everything from African art to beds to fetish clothing to antiques. This is probably the best place in London for interesting clothes, including vintage, goth, cyber and general club-wear. Cyberdog is an experience just to look at, and the extreme basement contains some distinctly adult items. Burleska and Sai Sai are among a number of

voyage.name: Camden Lock Village
voyage.content: The three-storey market that stood here burned down in 2008. It has reopened since, but the area just contains a number of small stalls. The owners are trying to get planning permission for re-development.

voyage.name: Inverness Street Market
voyage.content: This is a small market selling a range of common goods such as fruit and vegetables, cheap clothes and other bits and bobs. The Inverness Street Market is the smallest market in Camden, but it's the original local market in Camden predating the others by decades.

voyage.name: The Buck Street Market
voyage.content: This is the first market you see turning right out of the tube station and it has a big sign declaring it "The Camden Market". However, it only sells only the typical funny t-shirts, knock-off designer boots, keyrings, etc., that you can find in practically every city in the world.

voyage.name: Amsterdam London Shop
voyage.content: Probably the finest purveyor of curious things in London. They also sell weed and hash-smoking paraphernalia.

voyage.name: Official Doc Martens Boot Co.
voyage.content: Selling Doc Martens since the 1960s. The proprietor is always happy to talk and has some fun tales about the strange requests he has had from famous people.

voyage.name: Rokit
voyage.content: A proud upshoot that took its roots from Camden market and now has four high street stores across London.

voyage.name: The Harry Potter Shop at Platform 9¾
voyage.content: One-stop emporium for all your wizarding needs, this is the official souvenir shop of the Harry Potter franchise in London. Adjacent is the eponymous platform, where you can have your picture taken pushing a luggage trolley through a solid wall. It's probably the only other Harry Potter-themed store in London outside of the WB Studio Tour in Watford.

voyage.name: St. Pancras International Station
voyage.content: A selection of cafes at the station. Convenient for a quick bite.

voyage.name: Frida
voyage.content: Mexican cafe bar & bistro with vegetarian & Vegan options.

voyage.name: Ravi Shankar Bhelpoori House
voyage.content: Indian restaurant named after the famous Indian sitarist and composer. A superb vegetarian Thali can be had for under £10. Wash it down with a Kingfisher and you are set for the night.

voyage.name: The Devonshire Arms
voyage.content: The dress code is strictly alternative and the pub has got a late night license for Fridays and Saturdays. DJs every night and some gigs. The artwork on the walls was produced by Robin, the barman.

voyage.name: The Camden Road Draft House
voyage.content: Victorian Boozer

voyage.name: The Dublin Castle
voyage.content: A bit rowdy and often quite packed, this pub and music venue has played a pivotal role in British music. It is well known for producing the 1980s band Madness and helping a great many other groups along their path to glory. Worth a stop, just for the atmosphere.

voyage.name: The Edinboro Castle
voyage.content: A more refined side of Camden, this pub is part of a chain in North London attempting to apply a little class. It has a fine selection of beer and cider, including a selection of Belgian beers both bottled and draught. The food is always good and the staff always friendly. There is a large, semi-covered outdoor seating area with heaters.

voyage.name: The Good Mixer
voyage.content: A nice pub where the likes of Blur and Pulp and a load of other Britpop bands from the 1990s used to drink. Prices are reasonable, there are two pool tables, and the general atmosphere is laid back and friendly.

voyage.name: Hawley Arms
voyage.content: Tucked away in a side street close to the Stables Market, this two-story pub has a small garden and a roof terrace. There are sometimes concerts upstairs. A favorite of the late Amy Winehouse.

voyage.name: Jazz Café
voyage.content: Food, drink, and music (jazz, soul, blues). Every Saturday the place turns into a great 1980s music club, with "I love the 80s".

voyage.name: Waitrose's Wine Bar
voyage.content: Pleasant and good-value place to sit and sip, though it closes when Waitrose around 9PM.

voyage.name: The World's End
voyage.address: 174 Camden High St, Camden Town, NW1 0NE
voyage.content: Local landmark and a good meeting point. It is large, with two separate bars and a lot of seating. Food is served at the weekend.

voyage.name: The Lion And Unicorn
voyage.content: Pub with a Theatre

voyage.name: Neighbour
voyage.content: with Jukes Basement Bar: previously the Kentish Town police cells

voyage.name: The Oxford Tavern
voyage.content: Gastropub

voyage.name: The Euston Tap
voyage.content: in a classical Victorian Gatehouse

voyage.name: The Prince Arthur
voyage.content: A nice pub away close to Euston station.

voyage.name: The Rocket
voyage.address: 120 Euston Rd, Somers Town, London NW1 2AL

voyage.name: The Blues Kitchen
voyage.hours: Mon–Wed noon–midnight, Thu noon–1AM, Fri noon–2AM, Sat 10AM–2AM, Sun 10AM–midnight

voyage.name: Scala
voyage.content: Former cinema which was used in WWII to manufacture weapons and then faced a piracy lawsuit after screening A Clockwork Orange after Stanley Kubrick famously banned it. Now an alternative music venue.

voyage.name: Electric Ballroom
voyage.content: A historic ballroom turned contemporary rock music venue. As a former dancefloor, the audience stands on a flat surface so it may be difficult to see the stage further back. The Ballroom hosts several different club nights. It is a big venue with two separate dance floors and four bars. Features a rock floor, as well as a floor for the industrial/goth/rock/techno genres.

voyage.name: The Underworld
voyage.content: It is a great spot to go and catch alternative bands: goth, metal, electronica, rock, punk and many others are found here. Friday nights are also regular club nights, attracting large numbers from the young alternative crowd and more "studenty" than on Saturdays.

voyage.name: KOKO
voyage.content: Grade II listed music venue with restaurant. Card only.

voyage.name: Smart Camden Inn Hostel
voyage.content: Part of the Smart Backpackers chain of hostels, on the street next to Camden High Street.

voyage.name: St Christopher's Camden Hostel
voyage.price: Dormitory from £12 which includes breakfast and WiFi
voyage.content: On the corner of Camden High St and Plender St, which is home to a small morning market. Belushi's bar on the ground floor.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn London - Camden Lock
voyage.content: A modern hotel with 130 rooms beside the canal at Camden Lock.

voyage.name: Premier Inn London King's Cross
voyage.content: A modern, clean, reasonably priced hotel.

voyage.name: Pullman London St. Pancras
voyage.price: £200 gets you a room with breakfast on most days
voyage.content: It is equidistant from the St. Pancras and Euston railway stations. This former corporate Novotel was taken over and completely refurbished by Accor's upscale Pullman brand. It features rather spacious rooms and interesting views from upper floors, as well as modern decor and fitments and all the creature comforts expected from an upscale hotel.

voyage.name: St. Pancras Renaissance Hotel
voyage.content: This is the rebirth of the former Midland Hotel that operated the space from 1873-1935, inside the palatial heritage-listed Neo-Gothic St. Pancras station building above. Definitely outside the budget of many travellers, but for architectural aficionados this is one hotel that should be stayed in at least once in a lifetime. While the public spaces are original, the rooms are in a wing constructed in the 2000s, with

voyage.name: Great Northern Hotel
voyage.content: The railway hotel of King's Cross station, and the oldest of London's railway hotels, opened in 1854. The hotel is named after the Great Northern Railway, the company that built King's Cross station and operated it until 1923.

voyage.name: Crystal Palace Park
voyage.content: While the Crystal Palace is no longer there, the 200-acre park is a lasting reminder of the grandeur of the scheme. There is a wide range of things to see and do, including a hedge maze, a sports centre with Olympic-sized pool, a boating lake, fishing, an athletics stadium and an open air concert bowl by a lake among other things. The park is a great place for a walk and also for cycling around. A significant attract

voyage.name: Riverside developments
voyage.content: Developments of Shad Thames and Surrey Quays which contains numerous London Dock artifacts. Bermondsey St has undergone extensive redevelopment in the last seven years and it has been transformed into a highly desirable place to live and work.

voyage.name: St George the Martyr
voyage.content: Built in 1736, this attractive church is associated with 'Little Dorrit', the title character of a novel by Charles Dickens.

voyage.name: St Paul's Church
voyage.content: Built in 1720, it has been called A remarkable example of English Italianate Baroque.and often has classical concerts and organ recitals. John Betjeman is said to have called the church "a pearl at the heart of Deptford". Adjacent to the beautiful (and quite eerie at night) church yard is Albury Street, which has some fine 18th-century houses which were popular with sea captains and shipbuilders. Christopher Marlowe,

voyage.name: Sydenham Hill Wood
voyage.content: A remnant of the great hornbeam and oak woodland that once traversed South London. Run as a reserve by the London Wildlife Trust. Some splendid old trees and healthy bird and insect populations.

voyage.name: Southwark Park
voyage.content: A large, open and green park in an otherwise densely built part of London. Wide range of sporting facilities, a cafe, boating lake and an art gallery.

voyage.name: Tsar Peter the Great Monument
voyage.content: Tsar Peter the Great Monument, which is located at the waterfront adjacent to Deptford Creek and paid for by the Russian government to commemorate the cultural exchange between two great seafaring nations (it could be argued that Deptford Docks inspired the birth of the Russian navy). The writer and gardener, John Evelyn (1620–1706) who lived at Sayes Court, (now run-down and neglected) hosted the young, rowdy Peter

voyage.name: Brunel Museum
voyage.content: A museum dedicated to the works of the great engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel including a major exhibition about the founding of the London tube system. Also a fine collection of Victorian industrial paintings on show.

voyage.name: The Horniman Museum
voyage.content: A fine museum with an eclectic collection of stuffed animals, wonderful collection of world musical instruments, with interactive information. There is also an aquarium with an admission charge. A real hidden gem for those with an interest in the anthropology of African and Asian cultures. Pleasure gardens with a fine view over London, are adjacent to the Museum, perfect for a picnic on a fine day.

voyage.name: Dulwich Picture Gallery
voyage.price: £4, senior citizens £3, unemployed, disabled, students and children free, additional charge for special exhibitions
voyage.hours: Tue-Fri 10AM-5PM, Sat Sun and bank holiday Mondays 11AM-5PM; closed Good Fri, 1 Jan and 24-26 Dec
voyage.content: One of London's lesser known treasures showcasing a magnificent collection of old masters, including works by Poussin, Claude, Rubens, Murillo, Van Dyck, Rembrandt, Watteau, Gainsborough and many others. It was assembled for the King of Poland in the 1790s; an alternative home was found for the collection of artworks in the "clean air of Dulwich" after the Kingdom of Poland's partition and temporary disappearance as

voyage.name: Fashion and Textiles Museum
voyage.content: It's in the vicinity of Bermondsey Spa Gardens, and is an intriguing museum with those for a passion for fashion.

voyage.name: Imperial War Museum
voyage.content: It's in the former Bethlehem Mental Hospital (and the origin of the word Bedlam) in Southwark. Founded to commemorate the efforts of soldiers from Britain and the Empire in World War I, it has expanded over the decades with exhibits on World War II, more recent conflicts, and rotating exhibitions. The museum contains a vast array of military exhibitions including an eagle statue from Hitler's desk, and replica-shell

voyage.name: The Cuming Museum
voyage.content: The first gallery tells the story of the Cuming family and their collection the second gallery focuses on the history of Southwark and is split into three areas, settling here, a place to visit and world connections. The Southwark gallery looks at the people who have lived and worked here from Roman times to today. The third gallery in the museum is the temporary exhibition gallery - exhibitions change every four to

voyage.name: Rangers House
voyage.content: At Blackheath, maintains a large ceramic collection.

voyage.name: White Cube Bermondsey
voyage.content: Art gallery with exhibitions by major British and international artists.

voyage.name: South London Gallery
voyage.content: Long-standing free art gallery consisting of two locations across the road from each other. The work on display changes regularly, depending on what exhibition is on show, featuring current British and international artists.

voyage.name: Sands Film Studios
voyage.content: This film production company runs an informal cinema club which shows seldom seen and rare films. The club aims to disseminate a better knowledge of the history of world cinema. Club screenings are usually at 9PM every Tuesday. Attendance is free but you do need to join the club (also free and easily done by email - check the website).

voyage.name: Walk the Thames Path
voyage.content: Southwark and Lewisham host a large portion of the London section of the 184-mile-long Thames Path, organised by National Trails. The route between London Bridge and Deptford Creek largely follows the river (with occasional excursions inland), passing Tower Bridge, the Brunel Museum at Rotherhithe and Greenland Dock. Just north of Deptford, it cuts inland around the Convoys Wharf site before resuming its riverside ro

voyage.name: Bermondsey Antiques Market
voyage.content: A very famous long-standing market which attracts dealers from all over southern England every Friday morning. Antiques and collectibles from almost every imaginable genre. Used to be infamous for fencing stolen goods but that is no longer the case.

voyage.name: Deptford Market
voyage.content: The old working-class area of Deptford still has a lively street market, which is real and neither trendy or touristy! Likewise, East Street Market in Walworth, which has a real mix of African-Caribbean food stalls and antiques and oddities dealers. The birthplace of Charlie Chaplin is here, with several landmarks named after him.

voyage.name: Peter Layton London Glassblowing
voyage.content: A gallery, studio and shop which showcases contemporary glass pieces.

voyage.name: Lewisham Shopping Centre
voyage.content: Many high street chain retailers and a produce market outside too, plus H&M, M&S and TK Maxx department stores.

voyage.name: Cafe East
voyage.content: Wonderful Vietnamese food and if you like spicy authentic oriental food, this place is an amazing value.

voyage.name: The Sausage Man
voyage.address: Unit 1, St. Margaret’s Farm, St. Margaret’s Road, Dartford, DA4 9LB
voyage.content: Worth it for the name alone! This is a friendly mobile German deli, under Lewisham Clock Tower, serving the best frankfurters and bratwurst this side of Cologne.

voyage.name: A Torre
voyage.hours: T–Fri noon–2:30PM & 6–11PM, Sat noon–11PM, Sun noon–10PM
voyage.content: Portuguese restaurant.

voyage.name: The Yellow House
voyage.content: Informal restaurant and bar serving modern pub type food and a range of wood-fired pizzas.

voyage.name: Maggies Cafe
voyage.content: Below platform 4 of Lewisham train station, is a charming Irish café, extremely popular with the locals, which can make it hard to get a table come lunch-time. A mixed clientèle of City commuters and construction workers frequent this institution. They serve an all-day 'Make-your-own' fry-up for £6, where you can order what and as much as you like off a set-menu. Besides the traditional 'heart attack on the plate', t

voyage.name: Sapporo Ichiban
voyage.content: A very good and bargain-priced (by London standards) Japanese restaurant. On Monday to Thursday evenings (6-10PM) they serve £12 order all-you-can eat sushi and noodle dishes, which are freshly made by the experienced chefs.

voyage.name: Tai Won Mein
voyage.content: Offers fantastic Chinese cuisine, well, large portions at least, at a budget price. They only take cash.

voyage.name: A2 Lounge Restaurant & Wine Bar
voyage.hours: Mon–Thu noon–midnight, Fri Sat noon–2AM, Sun 5PM–1AM
voyage.content: Nigerian Restaurant - interesting if you want to try something different.

voyage.name: Planet 68
voyage.content: African joint.

voyage.name: Mekan Restaurant
voyage.content: It is an excellent Turkish restaurant, with a relaxed dining experience. Big generous portions.

voyage.name: The London Particular
voyage.content: Very good food at very good prices.

voyage.name: Chicago Grill plus
voyage.address: 315 New Cross Road, New Cross, SE14 6AS
voyage.content: Burger joint with many vegetarian and vegan options.

voyage.name: The Last Talisman
voyage.hours: Tue Wed 5PM–12:30AM, Thu noon–12:30AM, Fri noon–2:30PM, Sat 11:00AM–2:30AM, Sun 11AM–11:30PM, closed Mon
voyage.content: An Asian grill and bar opened in 2021.

voyage.name: Old Justice
voyage.content: A wood panelled pub with a good range of beers.

voyage.name: Old Salt Quay
voyage.content: River-side pub with great views across the Thames.

voyage.name: Ministry of Sound
voyage.content: World-famous nightclub with a reputation for strong DJs.

voyage.name: The Venue
voyage.content: is a night-club popular with the artsy crowd of nearby Goldsmiths University. It boasts 5-floors with a range of music from indie to techno, and houses cover-bands such as Bjorn Again. Lots of bohemian pubs are close by where up-and-coming bands (Athlete, Bloc Party and Art Brut all started around here) and DJ's ply their trade.

voyage.name: The Royal Oak
voyage.content: Serves excellent Harvey's beer, the only pub in London owned by that brewery, as well as delicious food. Classy selection of traditional British pub-grub along with more exotic choices, such as swordfish or crocodile. Routinely voted CAMRA London Pub of the Year

voyage.name: Camberwell Arms
voyage.content: Independent foodie pub famed for its Sunday roasts (rated #1 of 50 best Sunday lunches by the Guardian in 2017). Bars spread over two floors, great for either a drink or a bite to eat.

voyage.name: Stormbird
voyage.content: popular craft beer bar with broad, rotating range of interesting ales on tap

voyage.name: Blythe Hill Tavern
voyage.content: is a trad Victorian pub

voyage.name: Catford Bridge Tavern
voyage.content: is a newly refurbished up-market gastropub next to the stations, with 5 handpumps serving ales.Has a classy selection of gourmet food.

voyage.name: The London & Rye
voyage.content: is a cheap and cheerful Wetherspoons on Rushey Green named after a long-gone coaching inn, with a mixed crowd.

voyage.name: The Dog & Bell
voyage.content: A quiet old-time boozer, known for its fine selection of ales (usually 3 handpumps), above-average meals, and occasional regional beer festivals. Features a bar billiards table and sometimes live music (Irish folk music during the Irish beer festival, for example). There is a quiz on Sundays, and a performing arts venue across the street, in a converted brick warehouse.

voyage.name: Frank's Cafe at Bold Tendencies
voyage.content: A unique bar open in the summer months on the top floor of a multi-storey car park, with fantastic views over London.

voyage.name: Victoria Inn
voyage.content: Excellent restored Victorian pub with good food and stylish accommodation. No dogs.

voyage.name: Pasha Hotel
voyage.content: A unique place fronting Camberwell High St. It includes a central Asian restaurant, spa treatment and a shisha balacony, with views over the diverse neighbourhood below.

voyage.name: Church Street Hotel
voyage.content: Small beautifully decorated boutique hotel. Also the amazing Hotel Pasha is nearby.

voyage.name: Best Western London Queens Crystal Palace Hotel
Travelodge London Greenwich
voyage.content: Furnished place with funky design and cafe.

voyage.name: McMillan Student Village
voyage.content: Fantastic place for a good night's kip after a heavy night out.

voyage.name: DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel London - Docklands Riverside
voyage.content: On the South bank of the River Thames, the hotel has a great view of Canary Wharf.

voyage.name: NX London Hostel
voyage.content: Mainly multi-bunk bed dorm rooms with a few small private rooms

voyage.name: The Clarendon Hotel
voyage.address: 8-16 Montpelier Row, Blackheath Village, SE3 ORW
voyage.content: Rooms from £75, backs onto Blackheath, nice views.

voyage.name: British Museum
voyage.hours: Sat-Wed 10AM-5:30PM, Thu Fri 10AM-8:30PM; Central Great Court remains open Sat-Wed until 6PM, Thu Fri until 11PM
voyage.content: A vast repository of the world's cultures, controversially including hundreds of items that were looted from their places of origin. Entire sections are devoted to Egyptian, Greek, and Middle Eastern artifacts, as well as the piece which united them all, the Rosetta Stone. Other items on everyone's list are the largest collection of mummies outside Egypt and the Elgin Marbles. The collection also includes some of the

voyage.name: Cartoon Museum
voyage.content: A vast collection of cartoons and comics on display with special, often topical, exhibitions.

voyage.name: Charles Dickens Museum
voyage.price: £5, students and seniors £4, children £3, families £14 (two adults and up to five children), special group rates apply
voyage.hours: Mon Wed-Sat 10AM-5PM (last admission 4:30PM), Tue 10AM-7PM, Sun 11AM-5PM (last admission 4:30PM)
voyage.content: Museum at the former home of Dickens exhibiting writings, paintings, furniture and other items relating to the writer.

voyage.name: Foundling Museum
voyage.content: A museum and a gallery telling the story of the Foundling Hospital, an orphanage for abandoned children founded in the 18th century. Massive art donations by British artists and the involvement of George Friederic Handel as a patron made this childcare organisation an early centre of art and music.

voyage.name: Fitzroy House
voyage.content: A historic house that was inhabited by playwright George Bernard Shaw, it is where writer L. Ron Hubbard, founder of Scientology, worked in the 1950s. The building is reminiscent of the time, complete with Adler typewriters, Grundig tape recorders, and Western Union telefax. Tours by appointment.

voyage.name: Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology
voyage.content: Formerly the teaching collection of Sir Flinders Petrie, one of Britain's greatest archaeologists, now preserved by University College London. Exhibits include beaded dresses, sculpture and wall reliefs, items of everyday use, papyri, cartonnage and pottery. Fascinating!

voyage.name: Pollock's Toy Museum
voyage.content: A treasure trove of antique toys exhibited in a warren of 6 rooms above the toy shop of the same name. A very charming place indeed, though the doll rooms are a bit gruesome.

voyage.name: Wellcome Collection
voyage.content: Sir Henry Solomon Wellcome's vast collection of medical artefacts and art work that together explore what it means to be human. Special health related exhibitions.

voyage.name: Camera Museum
voyage.content: A downstairs museum dedicated to cameras from the 1800s to present day, including a camera rifle like the one used in Licence to Kill. The museum is a quick visit and worth the stop even for someone with a moderate interest in photography.

voyage.name: Brunei Gallery, SOAS University of London
voyage.content: An exhibition space that hosts a programme of changing contemporary and historical exhibitions from Asia, Africa and the Middle East, aiming to present and promote cultures from these regions and to be a student resource and public facility. There are live music performances every last Wednesday of every month except December and July.

voyage.name: All Saints, Margaret Street
voyage.content: An attractive Gothic Revival church, completed in 1859 to a design by William Butterfield.

voyage.name: All Souls Church, Langham Place
voyage.content: Completed in 1823, this attractive church near Broadcasting House is one of John Nash's masterpieces, with a prominent spire and circular vestibule. As of May 2025, it accessible only for worship.

voyage.name: Bedford Square
voyage.content: This wonderful square was built between 1775 and 1783 as an upper middle class residential area takes its name from the Dukes of Bedford, who were the main landlords in Bloomsbury. Distinguished residents have included Lord Eldon, one of Britain's longest serving and most celebrated Lord Chancellors. This is one of the best preserved set pieces of Georgian architecture in London and the majority of the buildings are

voyage.name: British Telecom Tower
voyage.content: 191-m (627-ft) skyscraper can be seen from far away and is the sixth highest building in UK.

voyage.name: Bloomsbury Square
voyage.content: This garden square was established by Lord Southampton in 1665 and is the oldest square in London. It was opened to the public in the 1950s. The square is surrounded by a number of beautiful 18th- and 19th-century buildings and terraces.

voyage.name: Coram's Fields
voyage.content: A park which is run as children's play area. Facilities include a pet's corner, lawns, sports pitches and a nursery. No adults are allowed to enter the park unless they are accompanying children. All visitors are welcome to join the local kids.

voyage.name: Russell Square
voyage.content: The largest square in London. It was established in 1806 by the 5th Duke of Bedford and his statue can still be seen in the square. There is also a café.

voyage.name: Senate House Building
voyage.content: Art deco headquarters of University of London featured in the film Nineteen Eighty-Four.

voyage.name: St George's Gardens
voyage.content: Peaceful gardens and interesting monuments including the daughter of Richard Cromwell, son of Oliver Cromwell.

voyage.name: Goodenough College
voyage.content: Goodenough College offers accommodation for international postgraduate students. The college's student community of approx 650 represents over 90 countries, offering a unique experience through stimulating intellectual debate, fostering cross-cultural activity and providing an exceptional social environment. Tours around the college are offered every Friday at 1PM and every first Saturday of the month at 11AM.
