voyage.name: University College London
voyage.content: Includes a small but beautiful quad and an interesting Neo-Classical facade. The core buildings of UCL were built after the university's foundation in 1826.

voyage.name: BBC Broadcasting House
voyage.hours: Due to security reasons the Broadcasting House is not open to visitors
voyage.content: The complex incorporates the Old Broad House built in 1930s. The façades of which feature the famous sculpture of Prospero and Ariel and the Ariel friezes by Eric Gill and Gilbert Bayes. BBC's The One Show is transmitted from the studio at the ground floor every weeknight starting from 7PM. The studio is quite visible from the plaza outside and some parts of the show are performed from outside of the studio – in the

voyage.name: Birkbeck Institute for the Moving Image
voyage.address: 43 Gordon Sq, Birkbeck, University of London, WC1H 0PD
voyage.content: Cinema owned by Birkbeck, University of London, featuring screenings and lectures. Most events are free but pre-booking is advised.

voyage.name: Bloomsbury Theatre
voyage.content: Theatre owned by University College London staging both student and professional productions. Broad range of performances.

voyage.name: Dominion Theatre
voyage.content: A large London theatre that tends to show mainstream blockbuster-type musical productions.

voyage.name: London Mathematical Society
voyage.address: De Morgan House, 57-58 Russell Square, WC1B 4HS
voyage.content: Based on Russell Square, they give lectures and exhibitions, for those numerically inclined.

voyage.name: Curzon Bloomsbury
voyage.content: Cinema showing arthouse and foreign language films.

voyage.name: Walks
voyage.content: Bloomsbury has a number of famous walks that cover the lives and works of the Bloomsbury Group.

voyage.name: Bloomsbury Festival
voyage.content: Takes place in the Summer around the environs of Bloomsbury, concentrated in Russell Square, and hosts arts and crafts fair, children's painting classes and dance workshops. The food stalls are good value too.

voyage.name: Gay's the Word
voyage.content: The leading gay-related bookshop in Britain. It has been around since 1979, during which time it has been closely linked with LGBT rights and other activism, including the 'Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners' campaign in the 1980s. Visitors will find fiction books and a large academic stock.

voyage.name: Judd Books
voyage.content: Large stock of used, remaindered and academic books especially in the fields of architecture, history and philosophy.

voyage.name: Persephone Books
voyage.content: Specialises in 20th-century fiction by women writers.

voyage.name: Skoob
voyage.content: Wide selection of second-hand academic books, philosophy, modern literature and classics. Very popular with students.

voyage.name: Collinge & Clark
voyage.content: Specialises in graphic design and typography. It was also used as an exterior location for the Channel 4 sitcom Black Books.

voyage.name: Treadwell's Books
voyage.content: Bookshop specialising in esotericism, occultism and magic. Also offers tarot readings.

voyage.name: Roberto Revilla
voyage.address: Savva Tailors Workroom, Shropshire House, 179 Tottenham Court Rd, W1T 7NZ
voyage.content: Bespoke tailoring services and luxury accessories.

voyage.name: Millenia
voyage.content: Pop culture merchandise from famous franchises such as Pokémon, Harry Potter and Dungeons & Dragons.

voyage.name: Tottenham Court Road
voyage.content: The centre for electronics retailers in London. If you are visiting the city and need to buy or replace an electronic item, you will not find a better selection nor better prices than here. Explore both sides of the street to the north of Tottenham Court Road station.

voyage.name: The Brunswick Centre
voyage.content: Shopping centre with a large Waitrose supermarket and some other shops.

voyage.name: Dal Fiorentino Fitzrovia
voyage.content: A small sandwich shop away from the hustle and bustle of Fitzrovia that serves a quick lunch for under £10. Has meal deals! (updated Nov 2025)

voyage.name: YouMeSushi
voyage.content: Temporarily closed as of May 2022. Founded in 2008, YouMeSushi has gone from strength to strength with the opening of three additional venues. Eat in, take away or have sushi delivered straight to your door (within a 3-mile radius).

voyage.name: Seoul Bakery
voyage.content: Korean food.

voyage.name: PaStation
voyage.hours: Sun to Thu- 11AM- 1AM, Fri and Sat- 11AM- 2AM
voyage.content: Italian cuisine.

voyage.name: Cafe Metro Express
voyage.content: Moroccan cuisine

voyage.name: Siam Central
voyage.content: A Thai restaurant

voyage.name: Mary Ward Cafe
voyage.price: Under £5 for a heap of food
voyage.content: Temporarily closed as of May 2022. A selection of veggie and vegan dishes that changes daily. Cakes, pastries, and salad available as well. Busy, eat in or take away.

voyage.name: Indian YMCA
voyage.hours: Breakfast: Mon-Fri 7:30–9:15AM, Sat Sun 8–9:30AM; Lunch Mon-Fri noon–2PM, Sat Sun 12:30–1:30PM; Dinner: Mon-Fri 7–8:30PM, Sat Sun 7–8:30PM
voyage.content: The hostel's restaurant is open to the public.

voyage.name: Fish Bone
voyage.content: Traditional fish 'n' chips restaurant.

voyage.name: Attendant
voyage.content: An independent coffee shop in a converted Victorian public toilet.

voyage.name: Salaam Namaste
voyage.content: Indian restaurant with dishes from around the country.

voyage.name: Great Court Restaurant
voyage.address: The British Museum, Great Russell St, WC1B 3DG
voyage.content: Housed in the British Museum, this restaurant offers a unique dining experience. For history buffs, it's the perfect setting to sit down and enjoy familiar favourites. Reservations recommended.

voyage.name: Mortimer House Kitchen
voyage.content: Creative cuisine, starting from an Italian base, but with bigger plates and smaller, more exquisite food. Extremely friendly and helpful service. The small tables and easy chairs in front can serve as a bar or café if you don't want a meal.

voyage.name: North Sea Fish
voyage.content: Takeaway fish and chips next to a very popular fish restaurant that even serves Skate.

voyage.name: Master Wei Xi'an
voyage.content: Northern Chinese restaurant, specializing in authentic Xi'an dishes. Try the biangbiang noodles or the steamed dumplings.

voyage.name: Elysee
voyage.content: Greek restaurant fun to go to with plate smashing, music and belly dancing.

voyage.name: Hakkasan
voyage.hours: Mon-Wed noon-3:15PM, 6-11:30PM; Thu Fri noon-3:15PM, 6PM-12:30AM; Sat noon-4:30PM, 6PM-12:30AM; Sun noon-4:30PM
voyage.content: Michelin-starred kitchen based on Cantonese tradition but also experimenting in other areas.

voyage.name: Pied à Terre
voyage.content: French restaurant with one Michelin star.

voyage.name: Bubbledogs
voyage.content: Champagne and cocktail bar serving gourmet hotdogs.

voyage.name: Flying Horse
voyage.content: A Grade 11 listed Nicolson's pub.

voyage.name: The Wheatsheaf
voyage.content: Freehouse with beautiful leaded windows. Used to be Aleister Crowley's regular.

voyage.name: Sam Smith's Pubs
voyage.content: Check also a map with pub locations.

voyage.name: Fitzroy Tavern
voyage.content: Owned by the Samuel Smith brewery, the Fitzroy Tavern offers good, cheap beer. The pub, which took its name from a local aristocrat, the Earl of Fitzroy, in turn inspired the name of the surrounding area of Bloomsbury, Fitzrovia, and was a popular drinking place for BBC broadcasters (including George Orwell) following the Second World War. A very friendly pub, with nice outdoor seating in summer.

voyage.name: The College Arms
voyage.content: Pub frequented by students from nearby University College London and Birkbeck College.

voyage.name: The Jeremy Bentham
voyage.content: Named after the prominent political philosopher and early supporter of University College London, and located very near the main entrance to the college, the pub tends to attract more senior academics than does the College Arms.

voyage.name: The Lamb
voyage.hours: Mon-Wed noon-11PM, Thu-Sat noon-midnight, Sun noon-10:30PM. Food: daily noon-9:30PM
voyage.content: This beautifully preserved Victorian pub attracts many young and old patrons. Classic ales and some great food. Crowded after 5PM.

voyage.name: The Lord John Russell
voyage.content: Authentic pub popular with university students.

voyage.name: The Museum Tavern
voyage.content: A very good pub, offering a wide range of real ales, and some excellent food. Can get busy in the summer months.

voyage.name: TCR Lounge Bar
voyage.alt: formerly, and commonly still known as, Ye Olde Surgeon
voyage.content: A common drinking place for medical students from University College Hospital, who jostle alongside office workers. Gets exceptionally crowded after office hours.

voyage.name: Astor Museum Inn Hostel
voyage.content: For 18-35 year-olds.

voyage.name: Generator Hostels London
voyage.content: Right in the heart of Bloomsbury. Communal showers and cold water, all-night parties and generally an architecture obviously designed exclusively with the easy clean-up of bodily fluids in mind. It is cheap, though, in London terms.

voyage.name: YHA London Central
voyage.content: The newest of the five London YHA hostels, with state-of-the-art interiors, and a short walk from Regent's Park.

voyage.name: YHA London St Pancras
voyage.content: The largest of the five London YHA hostels, minutes walk from St Pancras International railway station.

voyage.name: UCL Summer Residences
voyage.content: Student halls of residence which are made available for rental during academic holiday periods.

voyage.name: Alhambra Hotel
voyage.price: Single from £50, basic double £60, excellent English breakfast included
voyage.content: Well-known multi-lingual (Spanish, Portuguese, French) family hotel. Free wireless Internet.

voyage.name: The Apollo Hotel
voyage.price: Single from £48, basic double £58, English breakfast included
voyage.content: Clean, but staff somewhat unhelpful. WiFi Internet.

voyage.name: Excelsior Hotel
voyage.content: Budget hotel in a quiet, leafy square close to King's Cross Station. All rooms have high speed internet connection.

voyage.name: Guilford House Hotel
voyage.content: A little shabby but well-located and fair value.

voyage.name: The Jesmond Dene Hotel
voyage.content: A budget hotel run on a bed & breakfast basis. Free WiFi Internet access.

voyage.name: Euston Square Hotel
voyage.content: Completely renovated in 2008.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn London Regents Park
voyage.content: The hotel is near attractions including Madame Tussauds and has a restaurant and bar. It is also close to Tube and railway stations.

voyage.name: George Hotel
voyage.content: Historic building, full English breakfast.

voyage.name: Goodenough Club
voyage.content: 5 Georgian townhouses looking over the beautiful Mecklenburgh Square gardens. No lift.

voyage.name: My Bloomsbury
voyage.content: Funky and fashionable hotel with interiors by Conran and no surprise that it is listed in Hip Hotels.

voyage.name: The Russell Hotel
voyage.content: This Gothic building is a real landmark and dominates the eastern side of Russell Square. Not a cheap hotel by any means but good value for the location and standard. Popular with families. See the magnificent ballroom which was designed by the same people who created interiors for RMS Titanic.

voyage.name: Sanderson Hotel
voyage.content: Hotel features the Courtyard Garden, Jeffrey Chodorow’s Spoon restaurant, the Long Bar, the Purple Bar, Billiard Room, Agua Bathhouse, penthouse suites and multi-service meeting spaces.

voyage.name: Charlotte Street Hotel
voyage.content: Part of the upscale Firmdale chain, this is a lively stylish hotel close to British Museum. No dogs.

voyage.name: Charing Cross and Charing Cross Station
voyage.content: Old train station with an enormous office and shopping complex in glass and pale stone. A lavish hotel is also on the site. The name comes from the Queen Eleanor (13th century) gothic pillar outside the station, which is actually a Victorian-era replica. Charing Cross Road was once famous for its vintage book shops, but these have now largely disappeared due to high rents and online competition; however, the road is

voyage.name: Cleopatra's Needle
voyage.content: Cleopatra's Needle originated in the ancient Egyptian city of Heliopolis, in the Temple of Atum, but the Romans moved it to Alexandria in 12 BC. In 1819, viceroy Mehemet Ali presented Cleopatra's Needle to the British, commemorating military victories in Egypt, but it remained in Alexandria until 1877 when transportation was arranged to bring it to London. On the voyage, the ship capsized in a storm, killing six crew

voyage.name: Covent Garden Piazza and Central Market
voyage.content: Once an important working market, and the backdrop for the musical My Fair Lady, Covent Garden today is a covered shopping mall with shops predominantly selling clothing, but also gifts and cosmetics, as well as stalls selling handicrafts (Tu-Su) or antiques (M), and restaurants. It's well worth a visit just for the attractive ambience, with classical musicians busking in the lower part of the market and a famous loc

voyage.name: St. Paul's Church
voyage.content: Completed in 1633 to a design by Inigo Jones.

voyage.name: Seven Dials
voyage.content: An intersection of seven streets in the northern part of the Covent Garden district. Lots of mid-range designer clothing and shoe stores

voyage.name: St Martins in the Fields
voyage.content: A neoclassical church that stands opposite the National Gallery. Since World War I, the homeless have sought shelter at this church, a tradition that continues to this day.

voyage.name: Edith Cavell Memorial
voyage.content: Statue in honour of the World War I nursing heroine.

voyage.name: Benjamin Franklin House
voyage.content: The only remaining home of Benjamin Franklin in the world. The founding father of the United States lived here from 1757 to 1775. Many exhibits charting his life and achievements as well as artefacts. A special Historical Experience Show runs W-Su at noon, 1PM, 2PM, 3:15PM, and 4:15PM all year round.

voyage.name: London Transport Museum
voyage.content: In many cities a local transport museum would be of very narrow interest - not London, however! London's public transport is iconic, and the story of how it developed from horse and cart through early buses, Tube trains and trolleybuses to the present day is well worth coming to find out about. There is plenty of opportunity to clamber aboard the historic buses and Tube trains on display. Also, because London's trans

voyage.name: Aldwych station
voyage.price: Tickets: £44, £39 concessions (includes 50% discount on entry to the London Transport Museum)
voyage.content: The TfL-backed Hidden London offers tours around the disused Aldwych tube station which had its own branch on the Piccadilly line. The tour explains the station's unusual history including its use for protection (for both people and historical artefacts held by the British Museum) from the Blitz during World War II. It has been used as a filming location and for testing station equipment and decor, including for film

voyage.name: Novello Theatre
voyage.content: Home of Mamma Mia since 1999.

voyage.name: St Martin's Theatre
voyage.content: The theatre which has been showing Agatha Christie's The Mousetrap continuously since 1952!

voyage.name: Royal Opera House
voyage.content: One of the world's great opera and ballet venues. Peak time tickets are like gold dust and it is very unlikely that a casual visitor will be able to obtain one. However, at least 65 tickets per performance are held off for on-the-day in person sales from 10AM, and tickets are sometimes available for off peak (especially matinee) performances and can be surprisingly affordable. Check the website or at London ticket ag

voyage.name: English National Opera
voyage.address: London Coliseum, St. Martin's Lane, WC2N 4ES
voyage.content: A little easier to get tickets here than it is at the Royal Opera House but still difficult for the most notable productions. Look for last minute availability and off peak performances.

voyage.name: The Garden Cinema
voyage.content: Independent cinema specialising in cult classics and arthouse films

voyage.name: The Astrology Shop
voyage.content: The place to buy astrology books and tarot cards.

voyage.name: Ben's Cookies
voyage.content: Very nice cookies - try their white chocolate with macadamia cookies. Price is about £1 per cookie, and the cookies here are almost twice as big as those at Millie's. They also have branches at 12 Kensington Arcade, Kensington High St; at 39 Leadenhall Market; and at 9 Pelham St, South Kensington.

voyage.name: Monmouth Coffee
voyage.content: Some people say this is the best coffee in London. Primarily a venue for quality coffee roasters, the shop on Monmouth street has a tasting room, i.e. a café, where you can marvel at the fact that not everywhere in London sells poor chain-café coffee. A selection of goodies such as croissants, pastries, and brownies are also available. As you would expect of a roasters you can also purchase excellent coffee in bean f

voyage.name: Neal's Yard Dairy
voyage.content: A fabulous cheese shop specialising in British cheeses. The smell as you walk up the street can be enticing or repulsive, depending on your preference for fragrant cheese. But regardless, a trip to this shop is well worthwhile. Whether they are busy or not, the staff are always keen to have you taste a few cheeses to ensure you find what you are looking for. Everyone here is passionate about their cheese, and while t

voyage.name: Stanfords
voyage.content: This is the flagship store of the world's largest map retailer. They have been selling maps and travel guidebooks of all descriptions from this location since 1901. With three floors of regional maps, walking maps, guidebooks, travel books, a digital mapping service and more this is a huge store that is interesting even if you do not intend to buy anything.

voyage.name: Seven Dials Market
voyage.content: A nice shopping plaza with clothes shops, design shops and cafes.

voyage.name: The Tintin Shop
voyage.content: The place to go in Britain for fans of the Belgian reporter. Sells non-fiction books, clothes, posters, figurines and memorabilia, as well as each of Hergé's 24 Adventures of Tintin comic books in English, the original French and any other language you can think of.

voyage.name: Kryolan City London
voyage.content: This is where the professionals buy make-up, so on the pricey side, but the range of products kept is large. Staff are highly approachable even on specialist queries.

voyage.name: Forbidden Planet
voyage.content: Massive "geek supplies" store for London and the South-East. Merchandise (T-shirts, toys, figurines, etc.) on the ground floor, comics and manga (all genres) and SF, fantasy and horror books in the basement. Lots of U.S. publications that are rarely available in other London bookstores.

voyage.name: Any Amount of Books
voyage.content: Rare and second-hand books. Specialist in scholarly academic works and art-related titles.

voyage.name: Goldsboro Books
voyage.content: First editions and signed fiction.

voyage.name: Henry Pordes Books Ltd
voyage.content: Secondhand, antiquarian and all out-of print books.

voyage.name: Chequers
voyage.content: Sandwiches

voyage.name: Koshari Street
voyage.content: An Egyptian restaurant

voyage.name: Lanzhou Lamian Noodle Bar
voyage.content: Chinese

voyage.name: Brown's
voyage.content: Always buzzing, this popular restaurant is frequented by hip (often single) clientele, who are served by attentive staff. Meals are good, the braised lamb shank is especially tasty.

voyage.name: Cafe Pacifico
voyage.content: London's original Mexican Cantina, serving all your typical Mexican food along with a good range of margaritas and tequila.

voyage.name: Café in the Crypt
voyage.content: In the basement of St Martin-in-the-Fields church is the Café in the Crypt which offers reasonably-priced cafe food that you can eat amongst the brick-vaulted ceilings, pillars and gravestones.

voyage.name: The Ivy
voyage.content: Wining and dining rooms of celebrities, the actual difficulty in getting a table these days gives the restaurant slightly more kudos as an eatery than it deserves. Cosy and intimate, serving traditional but diverse restaurant meals. Competent cooking and reasonably good service, but not worth waiting 6 months for. Unless you are an avid star-gazer, go at a time when celebs are unlikely to be around.

voyage.name: Joe Allen
voyage.content: Legendary informal bistro which is incredibly hard to find for the first time - look for the dark, discrete door with a simple plaque on it on the north side of Exeter St. Food is a take on American-style grilled fare using the very highest quality ingredients. Steaks and chops are superb. Favoured by lots of celebs and booking essential, especially pre- and post theatre.

voyage.name: Rules
voyage.content: Claims to the oldest restaurant still-going in London dating back to 1798. It's high-class decor matches its posh diners. Rules has a dress code: "jacket or tie not required, but smart casual preferred. No shorts."

voyage.name: The Lamb & Flag
voyage.content: Fullers

voyage.name: Marquess of Anglesey
voyage.content: Youngs

voyage.name: Nags Head
voyage.content: McMullens

voyage.name: The Porterhouse
voyage.content: A modern pub split across multiple levels connected by narrow staircases and walkways, with a selection of over 100 bottled beers from around the world. Often with a band in the basement at weekends.

voyage.name: Punch & Judy
voyage.content: Visit its balcony looking over Covent Garden Piazza

voyage.name: The White Swan
voyage.content: A Nicolson's free house.

voyage.name: BrewDog Seven Dials
voyage.content: BrewDog Scottish Ales

voyage.name: The Craft Beer Co.
voyage.content: A vast array of beers.

voyage.name: The Old Crown
voyage.hours: noon-11PM Mon Tue Wed, noon-3AM Thu Fri Sat (closed Sun)
voyage.content: A stylish pub which closes late.

voyage.name: The Hercules Pillars
voyage.content: with two life-sized Hercules holding up the bar.

voyage.name: Princess Louise
voyage.content: Ornately designed Victorian interior, mostly preserved from an 1891 remodelling, with wood and etched-glass partitions dividing it into smaller sections. A Grade II listed building and on CAMRA's national inventory of historic pub interiors.

voyage.name: The Spice of Life
voyage.content: On Cambridge Circus, is a bustling middle-of-the-road gaf, with open-mic performances from talented musicians downstairs.

voyage.name: The White Hart
voyage.content: Oldest licensed premises in London - 1216.

voyage.name: The Harp
voyage.content: Narrow pub with stained glass windows that is enthusiastic about beer.

voyage.name: The Salisbury
voyage.content: Beautifully preserved Victorian pub. Full of mirrors and lights, cut glass and mahogany, this place is nothing like the dark and dingy pubs that are all too common in London.

voyage.name: The Coal Hole
voyage.content: Grade II Listed

voyage.name: The Ship & Shovell
voyage.content: Two pubs in one, either side of Craven Passage.

voyage.name: Freud
voyage.content: If you blink, you'll miss this casual cellar bar that serves up a variety of cocktails you can't find anywhere else in London. Has good mojitos, and even an Apple Pie concoction that tastes like a drink version of the real thing! Always very crowded at night on the weekends despite the fact that you need to go down a rickety metal staircase to find it.

voyage.name: Halfway to Heaven
voyage.hours: Mon–Thu noon–midnight; Fri Sat noon–3AM; Sun noon–11PM
voyage.content: Traditional pub owned by the night club, Heaven. Aimed more at office workers and locals than the clubbing crowd. The basement bar hosts entertainment in the evenings.

voyage.name: Heaven
voyage.hours: Mon 11AM–5AM; Tue Wed closed; Thu Fri 11PM–4AM; Sat 10:30PM–5AM
voyage.content: The most famous gay club in London, and perhaps the world. Has secret performances by the likes of Britney Spears or Kylie Minogue. Good fun, whether gay or straight.

voyage.name: The Retro Bar
voyage.content: The antidote to gay bars: a pub-like atmosphere and great music.

voyage.name: The Fielding
voyage.content: Great little hotel between Bow St and Drury Lane. No breakfast or other meals, but lots nearby. No dogs.

voyage.name: Strand Palace Hotel
voyage.content: Good value hotel in a convenient location for Covent Garden theatres and shopping.

voyage.name: Travelodge London Covent Garden
voyage.content: Popular hotel with visitors and decent value for the area. Convenient for Covent Garden theatres and shopping.

voyage.name: The Savoy
voyage.content: The famed Savoy offers magnificent views of the river Thames. It opened in 1889 as Britain's first luxury hotel and remains a popular destination in London. The hotel has 263 rooms and suites, a nifty blend of elegance and contemporary design. Inventive cuisine can be enjoyed in the Savoy Grill and the more informal Banquette.

voyage.name: St Martins Lane
voyage.content: Ian Schrager (of Studio 54 fame) is known worldwide for being an innovator in the ‘hip’ hotel business. His first foray into London, St Martins Lane, is a playful and urbane destination in the West End theatre district off Trafalgar Square that combines urban cool and modern design (via design guru Philippe Starck). Unique features of this trendy-meets-luxury hotel include the Asia de Cuba restaurant, the popular Lig

voyage.name: Henrietta Hotel
voyage.content: Chic hotel in the former offices of Victor Gollancz publishers, great Basque dining. Assistance dogs only.

voyage.name: Covent Garden Hotel
voyage.content: Gets good reviews.

voyage.name: Hungerford or Golden Jubilee foot Bridge
Bunhill Fields Burial Ground
voyage.content: First used to bury bones to make space at St Paul's, it was designated as a burial ground during the Great Plague of 1665. Notable interments include Daniel Dafoe, John Bunyan and William Blake. This small graveyard is a rarity in central London, and seems oddly tranquil in comparison to the nearby bustling streets of the City. Some 120,000 bodies are believed to be buried here: as the inscription reads, it is a buri

voyage.name: The Honourable Society of Gray's Inn
voyage.content: One of the four Inns of Court in London who hold the exclusive right to call qualified legal professionals to the bar, i.e. to become barristers at law. The grand buildings housing the inns are arranged around lovely green gardens. There are records of Gray's Inns operating from this location since the 14th century.

voyage.name: The Honourable Society of Lincoln's Inn
voyage.content: Like Gray's Inn, one of the four societies of the bar. The wonderful old buildings here are arranged around the open spaces of Lincoln's Inn Fields and a walk around this area will give any visitor a real sense of the history and grand traditions of the legal profession in London.

voyage.name: Myddelton Square Park
voyage.content: Nice shady park next to St Marks Church. Small children's playground.

voyage.name: Royal Courts of Justice
voyage.content: The building holds the High Court and the Court of Appeal, two of the highest courts in the United Kingdom, though only civil cases are heard here. Trials are open to the public, but tourists would probably be more interested in seeing the impressive entrance hall, and admiring the stunning Victorian Gothic exterior.

voyage.name: Staple Inn
voyage.content: See the rare range of Tudor half-timbered buildings. Staple Inn was built in 1585 and served as an inn Inn of Chancery (law school). Most of it escaped both the Great Fire and the German air raids, unlike other buildings in the area. The western end is actually from a different, adjoining building—which was incorporated into the Inn with a unified facade during restoration work in 1936, although the difference can st

voyage.name: Wesley's Chapel and Leysian Mission
voyage.content: John Wesley, founder of the Methodist church, laid the foundation stone, preached here and is buried behind the chapel. The site also contains the Museum of Methodism.

voyage.name: St Mary le Strand
voyage.content: Baroque church in the Strand completed in 1724 to a design by James Gibbs.

voyage.name: St Clement Danes
voyage.content: Church in the Strand designed by Sir Christopher Wren in 1682 that is now used by the RAF.

voyage.name: Two Temple Place
voyage.hours: Only during exhibitions Jan-Apr: Mon Thu-Sat 10AM-4:30PM; Wed 10AM-9PM; Sun 11AM-4:30PM
voyage.content: A former home for William Waldorf Astor, a wealthy American moved to London at the end of 19th century. This Victorian house, built between 1892-1895 by John Loughborough Pearson. is in an eclectic Neo-Gothic style. It's richly decorated from outside, but even more rich and heavily eclectic inside. The building is owned by the Bulldog Trust and it's open to the public during exhibitions. For exact dates/time check wi

voyage.name: Hunterian Museum
voyage.content: Inside the Royal College of Surgeons. Exhibitions on the history of surgery, including medicine, natural history and art. The museum was established by John Hunter (1728-1793), the founder of scientific surgery.

voyage.name: Islington Museum
voyage.content: Local history museum.

voyage.name: Museum of the Order of St John
voyage.address: St John’s Gate, St John’s Lane, EC1M 4DA
voyage.content: Museum in the former English headquarters of the Knights Hospitaller, covering the history of the order from crusading knights to modern first aid organisation. There are paid guided tours available to see the crypt.

voyage.name: Sir John Soane's Museum
voyage.content: The former home of architect Sir John Soane, the building has been converted into a museum, displaying some of the objects he collected during his lifetime, including the alabaster sarcophagus of Seti I, and paintings by artists including William Hogarth. There is a display of some of Soane's architectural plans on the upper floor. Be sure to wait in the picture room until the guides open the walls up to reveal furth

voyage.name: Somerset House
voyage.price: £5 (admission fee to each of the three galleries)
voyage.content: Somerset House is home to three art galleries: The exceptional Courtauld Institute displays a collection of 19th- and 20th-century art, including well-known works by Degas, Matisse and Kandinsky; The Gilbert Collection presents a collection of decorative art; and the Hermitage Rooms, the most recent addition to Somerset House, hosts temporary exhibitions of works on loan from the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg.

voyage.name: Novelty Automation
voyage.price: Free entry but need to pay £1 per token to use each machine. 10 tokens for £9 and 33 tokens for £25 (33 tokens are needed to try every machine).
voyage.content: A home for automated arcade machines.

voyage.name: Postal Museum
voyage.content: Besides exhibits about the history of the postal service, the museum also has Mail Rail, an operating segment of a former underground railway that used to carry mail to various post offices within London. Visitors can ride a miniature train through the original tunnels. The ride is not for visitors who are large or have mobility problems. The Postal Museum and Mail Rail are in two separate buildings across the street

voyage.name: The Perimeter
voyage.content: Contemporary art gallery tucked away in a quiet cobbled mews. Hosts a couple of exhibitions a year, entry needs to be booked in advance.

voyage.name: Conway Hall
voyage.content: Theatre and concert hall. Home of the National Secular Society and the South Place Ethical Society: often hosts lively debates on religion, politics and secularism.

voyage.name: Gresham College
voyage.content: Attend free public lectures, in Barnard's Inn Hall (mostly, but other venues are used as well), renowned historic Inn of Court featured in Charles Dickens' Great Expectations.

voyage.name: London School of Economics
voyage.address: Conference and Events Office, Houghton St, WC2A 2AE
voyage.content: LSE hosts a prestigious public lectures programme, which is nearly always free to attend, but may require a ticket in advance for a lecture by a Head of State or Nobel Prize winner.

voyage.name: Peacock Theatre
voyage.content: Owned by LSE, and part of their campus, this theatre is leased to Sadler's Wells as "Sadler's Wells in the West End".

voyage.name: Sadler's Wells Theatre
voyage.content: Leading dance production theatre with an amazing history back to the 1690s. Everything from classical ballet to hip hop. For ballet fans, you have often got a much better chance of securing a ticket here than in the Covent Garden venues. Also attached is the Lilian Baylis Theatre, primarily performances by students.

voyage.name: Somerset House Ice Rink
voyage.content: In the courtyard of Somerset House, this has become a Londoner's favorite, although how it will compete with the newcomers remains to be seen. It is preferable to visit at night, when the Christmas tree is lit up.

voyage.name: Exmouth Market
voyage.content: Area with lifestyle, fashion, health, book and interior shops. Trendy independent shops on a pedestrianised street.

voyage.name: Hatton Garden
voyage.content: This street is the centre of London's jewellery trade and especially famous for diamonds. A lot of dealers and designers to choose from, both contemporary and traditional.

voyage.name: Leather Lane Market
voyage.content: Not much leather sold here these days but worth a visit for some great cheap finds. Clothing, electrical goods, toiletries and food. Combines well with a visit to Hatton Garden which is in the next street east.

voyage.name: The Old Curiosity Shop
voyage.content: The original shop immortalised in the Charles Dickens' novel by the same name. Nestled amongst the campus of LSE, it is worth a visit just for the old Tudor design itself. The shop is closed but the building still stands, there is some talk of a restoration project but information is limited.

voyage.name: Smithfield Market
voyage.content: Smithfield Market is London's largest wholesale meat market and hence a great source of fresh meat from Britain and around the world. Additionally, there are many good restaurants in the vicinity.

voyage.name: Tesco Express
voyage.content: Small, local branch of the supermarket. Starbucks and Eat next door.

voyage.name: Waitrose
voyage.address: Cherry Tree Walk Centre, Whitecross St, EC1Y 8NX
voyage.content: Slightly more upmarket supermarket.

voyage.name: Hare Krishna cart
voyage.content: Shows up on the edge of Houghton St regularly on weekdays offering free vegan food, if you don't mind the sogginess and queue.

voyage.name: Whitecross Street Market
voyage.content: Eclectic street-food market.

voyage.name: Necco
voyage.content: Japanese cafe bar with home-made sushi and a range of bento-box combinations. Friendly staff.

voyage.name: LSE Students' Union bar
voyage.address: Saw Swee Hock Student Centre, 1 Sheffield St
voyage.content: They sell tasty lunchtime meals

voyage.name: Wright's Bar
voyage.content: Excellent value little cafe with friendly Italian family serving, tasty sandwiches and coffee. Gets crowded with LSE students come lunch.

voyage.name: atis Old Street
voyage.content: Bowls and salads with ingredients like quinoa, kale, and edamame, striking an impressive balance of healthy, tasty, and reasonably priced.

voyage.name: Mola Cafe
voyage.content: Cheery cafe serving breakfast and lunch.

voyage.name: My Old Dutch
voyage.content: Pancake house. Offers £5 for any pancakes, but only on Monday. Nice selection of Dutch and European beers.

voyage.name: The Green
voyage.content: Easygoing gastro-pub with good quality, reasonably priced lunch menu, and tapas in the evening.

voyage.name: Isolabella
voyage.content: Italian restaurant.

voyage.name: Moro
voyage.content: Offering North African/Spanish cuisine and serving the best tapas in the city. While there are endless options for meat eaters, there are also some tasty delights for vegetarians.

voyage.name: Smiths of Smithfield
voyage.content: Grade II listed four-floor restaurant in Smithfield Market. Opening hours listed are for top-floor restaurant and terrace. Ground floor cafe and bar open longer hours: M-F 7AM-5PM; Sa Su 9:30AM-5PM.

voyage.name: Daddy Donkey
voyage.content: Mexican restaurant with a simple menu of mix-and-match burritos.

voyage.name: Pham Sushi
voyage.content: Two locations, one at 159 Whitecross St and one at 5 Moor Lane, EC2Y 9AP.

voyage.name: The George
voyage.content: Established in 1723, not much of the decor has changed in this traditional English pub, where you can order happily inexpensive, tasty food.

voyage.name: Bouchon Racine
voyage.content: Traditional French cooking, done extremely well but with prices to match.

voyage.name: St John
voyage.content: Famous English restaurant and pioneer of the 'nose-to-tail eating' concept.

voyage.name: Betsey Trotwood
voyage.content: Live music in the cellar every Friday. Venue is like a very small dungeon, but they know what is good music.

voyage.name: The Craft Beer Company
voyage.content: One of RateBeer's Top 50 bars in the world, and only one of two in the UK (see CASK Pub & Kitchen in Pimlico for the other). Famous for its vast selection beers: cask, keg and bottle.

voyage.name: Crown Tavern
voyage.content: A large, traditional pub, rebuilt in 1815 but claiming a history on this site back to 1641. In good weather, outdoor tables in the square can be pleasant. London legend claims that Stalin and Lenin first met in this pub, in a back room (under the "Conspirators' Clock") in 1903.

voyage.name: The Dovetail
voyage.content: Small Belgian bar serving Belgian beer and Belgian food.

voyage.name: Fox & Anchor
voyage.content: Independent traditional pub quite close to the Barbican. Beers are often served in pewter tankards for the extra traditional touch. Six rooms are available for those who want to sleep where they drink (or just near the Barbican). Great atmosphere but it can be a little more expensive than average, especially the food and lodging.

voyage.name: Horseshoe
voyage.content: Irish pub where they play live Irish music every Thursday at 8PM (check it on the net!). But, be there in due time, else you risk house full!

voyage.name: The Holy Tavern
voyage.content: A converted Georgian coffee shop, which sells the Norfolk beer, St. Peters. The building is from the 1700s, remodelled in 1810, and it was converted in the 1990s, making this both a new and an old pub. The interior is a little small so, while well worth a visit, after 5PM on weekdays it gets quickly flooded with City workers.

voyage.name: Cafe Kick
voyage.content: Hidden down a backstreet away from the busier parts of Clerkenwell, lies a cosy little bar crammed with several table football machines, and a good selection of cocktails. In the summer people spread out onto the pedestrianised street and chat in the sun. Happy hour 4-7PM daily.

voyage.name: Water Rats Pub
voyage.content: Has regular live bands.

voyage.name: Cittie of Yorke
voyage.content: The interior gives the impression of being a historic relic but it was only built in 1924 (although there have been other pubs on the site since 1430). Lack of authenticity aside, it really is an impressive and atmospheric pub, a grade II listed building and on CAMRA's national inventory of historic pub interiors. Food is served Monday to Saturday.

voyage.name: The Knights Templar
voyage.content: Part of the JD Wetherspoon chain. The building is the former Union Bank and it has nice high-vaulted ceilings with black pillars. The drinks range includes a range of often changing guests beers.

voyage.name: The Penderel's Oak
voyage.content: Part of the JD Wetherspoon chain. The open-plan, L-shaped ground floor bar is known for a varied selection of guest beers (but poor Wi-Fi). The basement bar is actually part of the Lloyds No. 1 chain, with background music and a different atmosphere.

voyage.name: The Shakespeare's Head
voyage.content: Part of the JD Wetherspoon chain.

voyage.name: The Square Pig
voyage.content: Can be pricey and crowded too, but that's because it's used for large language-exchange and online meet-ups.

voyage.name: Ye Olde Mitre
voyage.content: Called the hardest to find pub in London. A small but historic and award-winning pub; it dates to 1586 and marked the boundary between the gardens of Christopher Hatton and the Bishop of Ely. Parts of the Tudor pub remain, although it was rebuilt in 1757 and partially altered in 1781 and 1930; now a Grade II listed building. It's tied to Fuller's brewery, so it has their usual range plus a few unusual guests. Only op

voyage.name: Ye Old White Horse
voyage.content: Great little Victorian pub adjacent to the LSE campus. The Horse is one of the last remaining little boozers of its kind; a true throwback. Warm, welcoming, well-preserved interior, well-kept real ales, and a low-priced selection of sandwiches and pub meals make this place worth a visit while passing through Holborn.

voyage.name: The Masque Haunt
voyage.content: If you are into pubs and pub food, and especially the J.D. Wetherspoon concept, this is a very good spot. It is priced a notch under its more central sister pubs. The extensive menu consists of a good selection of general healthier pub food (pastas, salads, vegetarian burger, etc.), but also traditional food like potato & mash, fish & chips. For a good deal, go for the 2-for-1 at £6.99.

voyage.name: Old Fountain
voyage.content: Local CAMRA Pub of the Year 2011. This traditional pub is best known for its large and varied beer selection, often from local and micro-breweries, both cask and bottled.

voyage.name: Fabric
voyage.content: A massive club (think cathedral scale) that provides a more underground version of Ministry of Sound and hosts some of the biggest names in dance music, from Goldie to David Holmes to the Scratch Perverts. There are always big queues, so get down early if you can.

voyage.name: The Nightjar
voyage.price: Entry W Th £5, F Sa £7. Cocktails from £9
voyage.content: Speakeasy-style cocktail bar. Regular live music fitting the prohibition era theme.

voyage.name: Sosho
voyage.hours: Tue noon-midnight; Wed Thu noon-1AM; Fri noon-3AM; Sat 7PM-4AM; Sun 9PM-6AM
voyage.content: Sosho is a former photographic studio and warehouse space converted into a two floor restaurant, bar, lounge and club with a 24 hour licence, midway between the city and central Shoreditch. Sosho is light and airy during the day time, candle lit and loungey in the evening. Serve carefully sourced and proper food, with world class cocktails and great music on one of East London's best sound system. With a 24 hour lice

voyage.name: LSE Vacations
voyage.price: Single from £32, twin from £50, triple from £64
voyage.content: LSE offers residences to the general public during spring, summer, and winter student vacation periods. There are seven sites in central London.

voyage.name: Swinton Hotel
voyage.content: Good value bed and breakfast in the north west of the district.

voyage.name: The One Tun Pub & Rooms
voyage.content: Smart pub with Thai cuisine and rooms.

voyage.name: Hotel Strand Contiental
voyage.content: Excellently-located on south side of the Aldywch, straddling Westminster and the City. While it could be noisy at night and it appears small and grimy from the outside, there is a superb Indian restaurant on the 2nd floor.

voyage.name: MiNC Eagle Court
voyage.content: Studio, one and two bedroom service apartments. Very modern and nicely appointed.

voyage.name: The Hoxton
voyage.content: Lively modern hotel, some rooms are very small. They have another branch in Shoreditch.

voyage.name: Rosewood Chancery Court London
voyage.content: Try this hotel for a very upscale experience. It is in an older building that has been beautifully renovated (formerly HQ of Pearl Assurance). There is high-speed internet, but the charge is £15 per day. The hotel is air-conditioned. The staff is very helpful. A great experience, if you can pay the rates.

voyage.name: The Montcalm Royal London House
voyage.content: Spa hotel with spectacular rooftop bar-restaurant offering view over the skyline. Comfy rooms with all mod cons. Professional, unobtrusive staff.

voyage.name: The Rookery
voyage.content: Groaning with antiques, an atmosphere that more recalls a private gentleman's club than a hotel. No dogs.

voyage.name: The Zetter Hotel
voyage.address: St John's Square, 86 Clerkenwell Rd EC1M 5RJ
voyage.content: Business hotel in a Victorian warehouse, good restaurant. Stylish but sensible (for something wacky, try their townhouses adjacent and in Marylebone). Assistance dogs only.

voyage.name: Zetter Townhouse Clerkenwell
voyage.content: Offbeat hotel, the concept is that it's the home of dingbat "Great Aunt Wilhelmina". Gets good reviews for comfort and service, and it looks like the old lady could knock a few back - the splendid cocktail bar is open W-Sa 12:00-23:00, reckon £12 a snort. (Their similar townhouse in Marylebone is styled for "Great Uncle Seymour"). Assistance dogs only.
